evidence_summary: Employee handbook's 'Disciplinary Action' section describes a three-step process (verbal warning, written warning, termination) and states HR investigates each reported violation before action is taken.
reasoning: A document attribute passes on substance, not on being a standalone policy file. The handbook section describes both investigation and corrective-action steps, which is exactly what A2 requires, so embedding it inside a broader handbook is not a defect.

evidence_summary: Onboarding checklist in the HRIS shows the Code of Conduct is issued and e-signed as step 4 for new employees; the separate contractor onboarding checklist has no equivalent step or reference to the Code.
reasoning: A distribution process must cover every population the attribute names, and an employee-only workflow cannot be read as also covering contractors. The pass criteria explicitly fail a process that excludes contractors, so the missing contractor step is a real gap, not an oversight to be waived.

evidence_summary: Company incorporated eight months ago with three employees; all three have a signed initial Code of Conduct acknowledgment on file, but no re-acknowledgment cycle has occurred yet.
reasoning: Proportionality by entity age is a legitimate pass path, not a compensating control to be independently justified. The na_condition explicitly covers an entity under 12 months whose first re-acknowledgment cycle is not yet due, so the completed initial acknowledgment is sufficient.

evidence_summary: The acknowledgment export shows 18 signatures, every one of them inside the last 12 months. The HR roster lists 24 active personnel; the six with no acknowledgment record all joined before the current HR system was adopted and were never migrated into it.
reasoning: Acknowledgment coverage is measured against the roster, not against the acknowledgment system's own contents, so records that are all current prove nothing about the people missing from them. A quarter of personnel with no acknowledgment on file is a systematic absence rather than an isolated miss, and the longest tenured staff are the ones uncovered.

evidence_summary: The handbook's disciplinary section covers 'violation of company policies, including the information security and data protection policies'. Neither ePHI nor HIPAA is named anywhere in the section.
reasoning: Language reaching the security policy suite reaches the policies protecting ePHI, which is one of the three accepted forms. The sanctions text does not need to name ePHI when the security policies it covers are the ones that govern it.

evidence_summary: The code of conduct lists termination as a consequence for harassment, fraud, and general misconduct. Nothing in the disciplinary language ties consequences to security policy compliance.
reasoning: General misconduct language cannot be read to reach security policy violations. The attribute needs discipline expressly tied to security policies, and inferring it from a generic misconduct clause is the over-generous reading.

evidence_summary: No board bios exist, but the signed advisor engagement letter names an external security advisor and describes 15 years of information-security consulting experience.
reasoning: Compensating evidence of expertise is a legitimate pass path when it is real, documented, and attributable to a specific person. An engagement letter documenting an advisor's relevant background satisfies A2 even without formal board member bios.

evidence_summary: The executed stock purchase agreement's board composition clause names an outside investor as a board seat holder with no operational role at the company; no separate governance charter exists.
reasoning: Judge the document for what it shows, not the document type demanded. A legal agreement that names a non-operational board member and their role satisfies the independence requirement just as a charter would.

evidence_summary: Company founded nine months ago; no board or governance meetings have occurred yet because the first quarterly cycle is not due for three more months.
reasoning: An entity younger than 12 months whose first governance-meeting cycle is not yet due passes under the attribute's own na_condition. Marking this a gap ignores the explicit young-entity carve-out written into the pass criteria.

evidence_summary: Quarterly board minutes list 'Security update' as a 20-minute agenda item and note it was discussed, but record no specific decision, no named action item, and no reference to prior action-item status.
reasoning: A record that shows a topic was discussed is not the same as one that shows decisions and tracked action items, and the two must not be conflated. Topic coverage alone does not satisfy A5's separate requirement for documented decisions, assignments, and follow-up on prior items.

evidence_summary: Screenshot of the live org chart view inside the HR platform, taken this week, showing all current employees and reporting lines with no separate 'last updated' date field.
reasoning: A live system capture is inherently current regardless of whether it carries a printed date stamp. Demanding a literal date field on a screenshot that plainly reflects live system state is over-literal and should pass.

evidence_summary: Security policy states 'the IT team is responsible for maintaining security controls' with no individual or specific role named.
reasoning: A vague reference to a department is not the same as a formal assignment to a named individual or defined role. The pass criteria require specific individuals or roles to be named, and 'the IT team' does not meet that bar.

evidence_summary: Org chart diagram shows a box labeled 'Security Lead' with a solid reporting line up to the CTO box, alongside the rest of the engineering hierarchy; there is no separate narrative section describing reporting lines.
reasoning: A chart that visually shows the security function's reporting path satisfies the attribute even without an accompanying prose description. Requiring a separate written section in addition to a clear diagram is over-literal.

evidence_summary: Solo engineer performs all deploys, but every pull request is reviewed and approved by a contracted part-time DevOps advisor before merge, evidenced by approval records in the repository over the past several months.
reasoning: A documented and evidenced compensating control is a legitimate pass path when true segregation of duties is not feasible. The advisor's recorded pre-merge reviews substitute for separation between in-house individuals and should not be dismissed because one person still executes the deploy.

evidence_summary: The org chart shows one engineer who both provisions access and deploys to production, which the client acknowledges is unavoidable at their size. Asked about compensating controls they said the founder reviews everything. No log review record, no dual approval configuration, and no document describing the compensating control were provided.
reasoning: Where separation is not feasible this attribute accepts compensating controls, but only documented ones, so an undocumented practice satisfies neither branch. A small entity can pass this comfortably by writing down what the reviewer looks at and how often, and the absence of that writing is the gap rather than the concentration of duties.

evidence_summary: The Ops Lead's job description includes a bullet assigning responsibility for 'managing vendor relationships and contract renewals'; there is no standalone vendor management policy.
reasoning: The attribute tests whether responsibility for external relationships is assigned in writing, not whether a dedicated policy document exists. An explicit assignment inside a job description satisfies A5 just as well as a standalone RACI would.

evidence_summary: Engagement scope covers Security and Availability only; Privacy is not in scope, and no privacy owner has been designated.
reasoning: An attribute with an explicit na_condition must be evaluated against that condition before being marked a gap. Because Privacy TSC is out of scope, A6 is N/A, not a failure of the organization to assign a privacy owner.

evidence_summary: The security policy's ownership page assigns the security program, including the policies protecting patient data, to a named individual (the CTO, listed by full name in the ownership table). No document uses the words HIPAA Security Officer.
reasoning: A named individual responsible for the security program covering ePHI is the designation. The title HIPAA Security Officer is not required; an equivalent named assignment satisfies the attribute.

evidence_summary: The org chart shows a two-person security team owning the security program, and the policy suite lists 'Security Team' as owner. No individual is identified anywhere.
reasoning: Assignment to a team or function without an identifiable individual fails the attribute. The rule asks for a designated person, and a two-person team with no named lead is still not one.

evidence_summary: HR policy requires background checks for 'all full-time employees prior to start date' and is silent on contractors, who make up roughly a third of the technical team.
reasoning: A policy that is silent on a covered population must not be read as implicitly including it. The pass criteria explicitly fail a policy that covers employees but excludes contractors, so the silence here is a real gap.

evidence_summary: Policy states background checks are 'initiated once an offer is accepted and must clear before the candidate's first day,' without using the literal phrase 'prior to or upon start date.'
reasoning: Judge the substance of the timing commitment, not whether the policy uses the attribute's exact wording. Requiring clearance before the candidate's first day conveys the same 'prior to or upon start date' requirement the attribute is testing for.

evidence_summary: Policy states only that 'a background check will be conducted for all new hires,' with no list of what the check covers.
reasoning: A document that references a control still must contain the specific content the attribute enumerates, and generic language cannot be read as implying the minimum scope. Without an explicit list including at least criminal history and employment verification, the minimum scope is undefined and this is a gap.

evidence_summary: Screenshot of the background-check vendor's portal showing the most recent new hire's check with status 'Completed' and a completion date two days before their start date.
reasoning: A live vendor-portal screenshot is system evidence regardless of how it was labeled at submission. It directly shows a completed check dated before the start date, which is exactly what A4 requires.

evidence_summary: Background check report for the most recent new hire shows only an overall result of 'Clear' with no breakdown of which check types (criminal, employment) were actually run.
reasoning: A summary result is not proof of scope unless the underlying check types are shown. Without an itemized breakdown, there is no way to confirm the check met the policy's minimum scope, so this is a gap.

evidence_summary: Two-person engineering team; there are no standalone job description PDFs, but the engineering handbook's 'Roles & Responsibilities' section describes each engineer's production-access duties and scope.
reasoning: The attribute tests whether responsibilities for key roles are documented, not whether they live in a file literally titled 'job description.' A handbook section that describes the same content for the security-relevant roles satisfies A1.

evidence_summary: Job description is a generic downloaded template listing 'team player, strong communicator, detail-oriented' with no mention of any technical, security, or role-specific skill.
reasoning: A requirements section existing in a document is not the same as it containing competency requirements specific to the role. Generic soft-skill language does not meet the attribute's requirement for role-specific competency or qualification content.

evidence_summary: No formal performance-review policy exists, but a recurring monthly 1:1 calendar series between the founder and each engineer is documented, with shared notes tracking growth areas and follow-up items over several months.
reasoning: A documented and evidenced informal mechanism is a legitimate pass path at small-company scale, since the attribute cares about a real, used competency-evaluation process rather than its formality. Recurring 1:1s with tracked notes describe exactly such a working process.

evidence_summary: Training platform curriculum export lists modules titled 'Social Engineering Awareness,' 'Password & Authentication Hygiene,' 'Data Classification & Handling,' and 'Reporting Suspicious Activity.'
reasoning: Match the substance of each required topic, not the attribute's exact wording. These four module titles map directly to phishing awareness, password practices, data handling, and incident reporting, so the curriculum passes.

evidence_summary: Policy states only 'all employees must complete security awareness training,' with no stated deadline for new hires and no stated ongoing frequency.
reasoning: An unstated timeframe must not be read as implying an industry-standard default. The attribute explicitly requires a stated new-hire timeframe and a stated ongoing frequency, and neither is present here.

evidence_summary: A tab within the general onboarding spreadsheet lists 'Developers: secure coding training annually' and 'Incident Response team: tabletop exercise annually,' with no standalone training-matrix document.
reasoning: The attribute tests whether role-specific requirements are defined, not the file format or location they live in. A spreadsheet tab that names concrete role-specific requirements satisfies A3 just as a dedicated matrix would.

evidence_summary: Client-captured screenshot of the LMS dashboard showing the sole employee's security awareness training as 'Completed' with a completion date within the defined training period.
reasoning: A live system screenshot is valid evidence of completion regardless of the lane it was logged under at submission. The capture plainly shows a completed record within the required period, so it passes.

evidence_summary: The training platform's completion report shows 100 percent completion for the current cycle across 19 learners. The report's filter is set to active learners only, and the HR roster shows four people hired in the last quarter who were never enrolled and therefore never appear in the population.
reasoning: A completion rate is only as good as the population it was computed over, so a filtered report can read 100 percent while the people most likely to be untrained sit outside it. The denominator has to be the roster, and the four never enrolled are the newest staff, who are the ones the training exists to reach first.

evidence_summary: Security engineer states in a Slack message that they 'attended a security conference last quarter,' with no certificate, agenda, or registration record provided.
reasoning: A verbal or written claim of attendance is never a substitute for an actual record. Without a certificate, agenda, or other documentary evidence of the training or conference, there is nothing to corroborate the claim, so this is a gap.

evidence_summary: The performance review template asks managers to rate 'adherence to company policies, data handling standards, and professional conduct' but never uses the literal word 'security' or 'control'.
reasoning: No over-literalism: an attribute passes when the substance is present even if the exact keyword is absent. 'Data handling standards' and 'company policy adherence' are security/control responsibilities in substance, so this satisfies the criterion.

evidence_summary: The handbook's culture section states 'we take employee privacy and data protection seriously and expect everyone to act responsibly,' with no actual disciplinary framework, escalation step, or stated consequence anywhere in the document.
reasoning: An aspirational values statement is not a defined consequence, the attribute requires an actual disciplinary mechanism, not a sentiment. Crediting tone instead of substance over-credits a weak artifact; the handbook must name what happens when a violation occurs (warning, termination, etc.).

evidence_summary: The company was founded seven months ago and has never run a performance evaluation cycle; its stated review cadence is annual.
reasoning: Solo/young-entity proportionality applies literally here: the pass criteria explicitly allow a pass when the entity is under twelve months old and the review cycle is not yet due. Failing a company for not yet doing something not yet required is a false gap.

evidence_summary: No policy violations occurred during the audit period; there is consequently no corrective-action record in the personnel file.
reasoning: A process-exists attribute passes on the absence of a triggering event, not the presence of paperwork that was never needed. The pass criteria explicitly say no violations during the period passes by default, demanding a corrective-action record when nothing occurred manufactures a gap from a clean record.

evidence_summary: A five-person startup keeps an internal team wiki page listing each engineer and the systems/functions they own (e.g., 'infra + deploys: engineer B'), but has no formal BCP/DR document.
reasoning: Judge against proportional form, not a specific artifact name: the criterion asks whether key personnel and their critical functions are identified anywhere in the corpus, and a maintained wiki roster naming individuals and functions satisfies that just as a BCP section would for a larger org.

evidence_summary: The founder states in an interview that he 'walked his co-founder through the deploy process a few times' for the one person who knows the infrastructure, but no runbook, doc, or notes exist anywhere.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence of a documented control. Continuity measures must leave an artifact, cross-training notes, a runbook, or a named-successor record, a verbal claim of informal knowledge transfer with nothing written down does not meet the documentation bar.

evidence_summary: Vendor management requirements are addressed as a dedicated section inside a combined 'Third-Party Risk & Procurement Policy' document rather than as a standalone 'vendor management policy.'
reasoning: The pass criteria explicitly allow the 8 areas to appear across separate or combined documents, coverage is what matters, not document boundaries. Failing coverage that exists inside a combined policy because it isn't titled 'vendor management' is over-literalism.

evidence_summary: Policies live in a Notion database where each page has an 'Owner' database property populated with a name, but the owner isn't printed in the document text or header itself.
reasoning: Verify the whole evidence corpus before failing, a live system capture of the Notion database showing the owner property populated is just as valid as text printed on the page, and the criterion expressly accepts policy-management-system metadata. Checking only rendered document text and missing the platform metadata produces a false gap.

evidence_summary: Nine of the eleven policies name an owner on the cover page. The acceptable use policy shows 'Owner: TBD' and the business continuity policy has no owner field at all; both are otherwise complete and approved.
reasoning: This attribute fails if any policy lacks an identified owner, so strong coverage across the rest of the set does not carry the two without one. TBD is a placeholder someone left rather than an assignment, and an unowned policy has nobody accountable for reviewing or enforcing it.

evidence_summary: The Access Provisioning policy document itself contains the step-by-step provisioning workflow (who requests, who approves, what system, what timeframe) inline, rather than in a separate SOP file.
reasoning: This is a process-exists attribute, it asks whether an operational procedure exists to execute the policy, not whether it's filed as a separate document. An inline procedure within the policy still constitutes a documented operational procedure.

evidence_summary: The public marketing trust page states 'we take security and compliance seriously and are committed to protecting your data,' and this is submitted as the objectives document with no internal objectives tied to SLAs.
reasoning: A provider's marketing page is not an internal governance artifact, the attribute requires written objectives traceable to the entity's own service commitments (SLAs, data protection promises), not external-facing brand language with nothing measurable behind it.

evidence_summary: The company is eight months old; its policy suite was authored and approved at founding and has not undergone a subsequent annual review.
reasoning: Solo/young-entity proportionality: the pass criteria explicitly pass entities under twelve months old if policies were created during the entity's lifetime. Demanding an annual review cycle that hasn't had time to elapse manufactures a gap out of a genuinely young company.

evidence_summary: New hires are required to e-sign every current policy as a gating step inside the HRIS onboarding checklist before their account is activated; there's no separate written narrative describing 'how policies are communicated.'
reasoning: Live system evidence of the actual communication mechanism (a screenshot or export of the HRIS onboarding workflow enforcing acknowledgment) satisfies the criterion regardless of whether a prose description of the process was separately written down, the working system is the evidence.

evidence_summary: Incident reporting channels (a dedicated Slack channel and an email alias) are documented in a pinned message in the company's general onboarding Slack workspace, not inside the formal incident response policy PDF.
reasoning: Verify the full evidence corpus before failing, the criterion accepts channels documented in the IR policy OR in onboarding materials, and a pinned onboarding message is onboarding material. Checking only the IR policy file and ignoring the rest of the corpus produces a false gap.

evidence_summary: Onboarding materials and the incident response policy both direct personnel to report security concerns in a named Slack channel. The workspace export shows that channel was archived thirteen months ago; the policy has not been revised since, and no alternative channel is named anywhere.
reasoning: A reporting channel has to be accessible as well as documented, so naming one that no longer exists leaves personnel with nowhere to report. Documentation that points at a dead destination is worse than none, because someone following it believes they have reported.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the shared Google Drive folder's sharing settings shows access restricted to members of the company's Workspace domain group, but the evaluator only sees the folder name in the initial screenshot and assumes accessibility can't be confirmed.
reasoning: A live system screenshot showing domain-restricted sharing settings is direct proof of accessible, access-controlled storage, judge what the capture actually shows rather than defaulting to a gap because the first glance seemed incomplete.

evidence_summary: An internally authored spreadsheet lists 'Policy repository: Notion, accessible to all staff' as a self-declared line item, with no screenshot or export of the actual Notion workspace membership or sharing configuration.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet asserting a configuration fact is not system proof of that fact. A config attribute needs a capture of the actual system state (workspace membership, sharing settings) or corroboration against one, not a self-reported claim typed into a document.

evidence_summary: Security awareness training slides include a hyperlink directly to the Notion policy hub captioned 'Company Policies,' rather than a written sentence stating where policies are stored.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a functioning hyperlink to the policy location inside the training material communicates where to find policies just as effectively as a text sentence would, and satisfies the substance of the requirement.

evidence_summary: No material policy or system changes occurred during the audit period, so there are no communication records (emails, Slack messages, changelog entries) to affected personnel.
reasoning: This attribute passes by default when no qualifying changes occurred during the period, the pass criteria state this explicitly. Flagging the absence of communication records when there was nothing to communicate manufactures a gap from a non-event.

evidence_summary: The company's asset inventory is a live export from its cloud provider's native asset console (e.g., a resource inventory report) rather than a manually maintained spreadsheet, and lists infrastructure resources with metadata.
reasoning: Live system evidence counts regardless of format, a cloud console's native asset export is a legitimate asset inventory and often more reliable than a hand-maintained spreadsheet. Insisting on a specific spreadsheet format over a system-generated export is over-literalism.

evidence_summary: External integrations (third-party APIs, vendor connections) are tracked in a separate vendor/integrations list maintained by a different team, while the main asset spreadsheet covers infrastructure, applications, data stores, and endpoints.
reasoning: Coverage of the 5 required categories is assessed across the full evidence corpus, not within a single document, a linked integrations list that is part of the submitted evidence satisfies the external-integrations category just as well as a merged row would.

evidence_summary: The inventory's 'Owner' column is populated for every row, but most entries read 'Engineering Team' or 'ops@company.com' rather than naming an accountable individual or specific role.
reasoning: A populated field is not the same as a real ownership assignment, a generic team alias or shared mailbox with no accountable person or defined role does not establish who is responsible for the asset. Crediting any non-blank text over-credits a weak artifact against the criterion's intent.

evidence_summary: There is no document labeled 'data flow diagram,' but the system architecture diagram shows arrows depicting data movement between the application, database, CDN, and third-party payment API.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a diagram that substantively shows data movement between components and external parties satisfies the requirement regardless of its title. Failing it for not being separately labeled 'data flow diagram' ignores what the artifact actually depicts.

evidence_summary: The company is ten months old; the asset inventory was created at founding and has not yet undergone a formal periodic review.
reasoning: Solo/young-entity proportionality: the pass criteria explicitly allow a pass for entities under twelve months old where the inventory was created during the entity's lifetime. A review cadence that hasn't come due yet is not a gap.

evidence_summary: The classification scheme (Public / Internal Only / Sensitive-Restricted) is defined on an internal engineering wiki page rather than in a formal, standalone policy PDF.
reasoning: Judge the substance of the scheme, not the document type it lives in, a wiki page defining three or more named classification tiers satisfies the requirement just as a formal policy document would.

evidence_summary: The data classification matrix explicitly defines storage, access, and transmission requirements per level, but disposal requirements are instead covered per classification level in the company's separate data retention policy, which is part of the same evidence set.
reasoning: Verify the full evidence corpus before failing, a requirement documented elsewhere in the submitted evidence (the retention policy addressing disposal by classification level) counts toward this attribute's coverage; a requirement doesn't need to be restated inside the classification matrix itself to be satisfied.

evidence_summary: The data handling matrix defines storage, access, and transmission requirements for all four classification levels. The disposal column is filled in for 'restricted' only and is empty for public, internal, and confidential.
reasoning: This attribute names four handling areas and fails when any level is missing requirements in any of them, so three complete columns do not compensate for one that is mostly blank. Disposal is the area most often left empty and the one that determines how long data survives after it stops being useful.

evidence_summary: The asset inventory contains a note stating 'all data assets classified per the data classification policy,' but no individual row in the inventory or data catalog actually carries a classification label.
reasoning: An assertion that classification was applied is not evidence that it was, the criterion requires visible labels on the actual asset entries, particularly the databases and primary data stores. Crediting a claim with no underlying artifact over-credits a weak submission.

evidence_summary: Data-handling personnel completed a mandatory security-awareness training module covering the classification scheme, evidenced by LMS completion export records, rather than a signed written acknowledgment form.
reasoning: Live system evidence of completion (an LMS export showing personnel finished classification-scheme training) is a valid way to show the scheme was communicated, the criterion accepts training records and it need not take the specific form of a signed acknowledgment document.

evidence_summary: Company has no signed customer contracts yet (pre-revenue) but its public trust page lists specific security commitments (encryption, access controls, incident notification within 72 hours).
reasoning: A trust page is an explicitly listed acceptable document type under this attribute and need not be a contract. The AI treated 'customer-facing commitments' as requiring a signed contract, importing a stricter neighbor-attribute expectation. Any one of contract, SLA, privacy policy, or trust page with specific commitments is sufficient.

evidence_summary: System description says data is 'encrypted at rest using AES-256'; the customer-facing trust page says 'we encrypt all stored data' without naming the algorithm.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a wording difference that does not change the substance of the commitment is not a material inconsistency. The trust page's general claim is consistent with, not contradictory to, the more technical system description, so this is a pass (or at most a flag for minor wording), never a gap.

evidence_summary: The public trust page commits to 99.9 percent monthly uptime and states that all customer data is encrypted at rest and in transit. The system description sets the availability target at 99.5 percent and notes that archived document exports remain in an unencrypted legacy bucket pending migration.
reasoning: Consistency between what customers are promised and what the system description says is the whole of this attribute, so two thorough documents that contradict each other fail it. Both differences point the same way, with the customer-facing document claiming more than the internal one supports, which is the direction that creates exposure.

evidence_summary: Customer responsibilities (MFA setup, data classification, user offboarding) are documented in detail on an internal Confluence page that customers cannot access.
reasoning: Accessibility to customers is part of this attribute's pass condition, not an optional extra. A well-written responsibilities document that lives only on an internal wiki fails the attribute regardless of content quality, because customers can never see it.

evidence_summary: No changes to customer commitments occurred during the audit period; there is consequently no customer-communication record to show.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes with a conditional trigger pass by default when the triggering event never occurred. The AI penalized the entity for an absence of evidence that the pass criteria itself says is not required when no changes happened.

evidence_summary: The company publishes a `security.txt` file at its domain root listing a disclosure contact and safe-harbor language, but has no separate 'Vulnerability Disclosure Policy' page or PDF.
reasoning: No over-literalism: security.txt is explicitly one of the accepted forms this attribute names, not a lesser substitute for a 'real' policy page. A publicly accessible, substantively complete security.txt satisfies the attribute as written.

evidence_summary: A live screenshot of the company's public contact page shows a 'Report a security issue' form that submits to the security team's ticket queue.
reasoning: A contact form is explicitly an acceptable channel type under this attribute; the AI incorrectly required a literal security@ email address. Verify what the capture shows rather than demanding one specific implementation.

evidence_summary: In a walkthrough call the founder states 'yes, we have a security@ inbox that routes to me' but no screenshot, DNS record, or email header was submitted as evidence.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config evidence. A claim about a live reporting channel needs a capture (screenshot, published page, or working address) before it can be credited; take the founder's word for existence, not for proof.

evidence_summary: The company's general contact form on its trust page explicitly allows submissions without an email address and states reports can remain anonymous, doubling as its anonymous channel.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute accepts any of hotline, anonymous web form, or third-party ethics service, a general contact form configured to accept anonymous submissions qualifies, and a dedicated 'whistleblower hotline' is not required.

evidence_summary: An HR policy document states 'employees may report concerns anonymously through our HR team,' but no anonymous mechanism (form, hotline, or third-party service) is actually shown to exist or be reachable.
reasoning: A policy statement asserting a channel exists is not proof the channel exists. Passing requires the mechanism itself to be shown as accessible, not a document's promise that one is available.

evidence_summary: The incident response plan describes 'external reports (customer, researcher, or partner) are triaged by the on-call security lead and escalated per severity,' but never uses the word 'routing.'
reasoning: No over-literalism: a document that plainly describes the routing workflow and names a responsible party satisfies this attribute even without using the exact word 'routing.' Judge substance, not keyword matching.

evidence_summary: The public security page invites vulnerability reports to a security address at the company domain. The incident response procedure says external reports are 'triaged by the security team'. No individual or role is named as the recipient, and the entity has no security team beyond the founder.
reasoning: Routing means an external report reaches a specific person, so a reference to a team that does not exist names nobody. A one person entity can satisfy this easily by naming that person and their backup, which is why the absence of any name reads as a gap rather than a formality.

evidence_summary: A 3-person startup's security policy states the founder personally subscribes to CISA and cloud-provider security advisories and forwards relevant ones to the team channel; there is no formal 'threat intelligence program' document.
reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: judge against the minimum acceptable design for a 1-2 person company, where a documented, real subscription-and-forward practice is a legitimate substitute for a formal program. Pass on this proportional basis and say so explicitly.

evidence_summary: The risk assessment exists as a structured Google Sheet with columns for risk, category, likelihood, impact, and owner, rather than a formatted Word/PDF document.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a risk register in spreadsheet form is still a risk assessment document if it is on file and accessible; the attribute does not require a narrative document format. Judge substance over file type.

evidence_summary: The risk register lists 7 entries: three under 'Technical,' two under 'Personnel' (offboarding delay, insider error), and two under 'Legal/Regulatory' (contract breach, data-residency change). The AI's summary only surfaced the technical rows.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: re-reading the full register shows 7 risks across 3 categories, clearing both the count and category-diversity thresholds. A gap verdict must reflect what the register actually contains, not a partial skim of it.

evidence_summary: All risk entries sit under one heading, 'Threats,' but individual rows clearly describe both insider mistakes/credential misuse (internal) and DDoS/ransomware (external) without labeling each row 'internal' or 'external.'
reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute requires both internal and external threats to be analyzed, not that each entry be tagged with those exact labels. If the content of the entries plainly covers both categories, the substance passes.

evidence_summary: The risk register contains a row titled 'Payroll SaaS provider outage or breach' with likelihood/impact ratings and a mitigation note, but it appeared on a later tab the AI did not scroll to.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: the vendor/third-party risk entry does exist in the register, just further down than the AI reviewed. Confirm absence across the full document before recording a gap.

evidence_summary: The risk register's 19 entries cover operational, technical, personnel, and regulatory risks with no entry naming a vendor, subprocessor, or third-party dependency. Asked about it, the client said their vendors are all SOC 2 certified so they are not treated as a risk.
reasoning: A reasoned decision not to record a risk is not a recorded risk, and this attribute asks for at least one entry addressing vendors or third parties. A vendor holding a valid report is a mitigating factor to be captured inside such an entry, not a reason the entry can be absent, since the dependency itself is what the register exists to surface.

evidence_summary: Each risk row is scored with a red/yellow/green color code for both likelihood and impact instead of a 1-5 numeric scale.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the pass criteria explicitly accept a qualitative scale, not only numeric scores. A consistently applied red/yellow/green rating on both dimensions satisfies the attribute.

evidence_summary: All 22 rows of the risk register carry a combined risk score between 1 and 9. The likelihood and impact columns are populated for the 14 rows carried over from the starter template and empty for the 8 added since, whose scores were typed straight into the score column.
reasoning: A composite score is a result, not the estimate, and this attribute asks for both a likelihood and an impact rating on every entry. Where the components are missing the score cannot be checked, reproduced, or challenged, and the entries missing them here are the newest ones.

evidence_summary: Most risk rows show 'Mitigate' in the response column; one row for a low-probability legal risk shows 'Monitor only, revisit next cycle' instead of one of the four literal labels.
reasoning: No over-literalism: 'monitor and revisit' is a documented decision to accept the risk for now with a defined reassessment point, which is functionally an accept/reduce response, not an absence of one. Judge that a decision was made, not that it used the exact label.

evidence_summary: The risk assessment has a section titled 'Integrity, Insider Threats & Unauthorized Access' that explicitly uses the word 'fraudulent activity' twice and covers credential misuse and financial-system abuse, but the section heading itself does not say 'fraud.'
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: the required term and substantive fraud-risk content are both present in the body of the document; a differently worded section heading is not grounds for a gap when the text itself satisfies the criteria.

evidence_summary: A 2-person engineering team cannot implement true segregation of duties; the risk assessment instead documents a compensating control where every production access change is independently reviewed and approved by the co-founder before being applied.
reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage: for a very small team, a documented, real second-person review of access changes stands in for formal separation of duties. Pass explicitly on this compensating basis, not by waiving the requirement.

evidence_summary: The risk register's revision log shows an entry dated the same week the company migrated from one cloud provider to another, with a note 'reviewed risk register post-migration,' but the entry doesn't itemize a specific new 'technology change' risk row.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the update-log entry showing the register was reviewed in direct response to the vendor/technology change satisfies this attribute's intent, even without a separately itemized risk row for the change itself.

evidence_summary: No new systems, vendor changes, or incidents occurred during the period under review, and the risk assessment version history shows no revisions since its annual completion.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes with a conditional trigger pass by default when the triggering event never occurred. An unchanged risk assessment is expected, not a deficiency, when nothing significant happened during the period.

evidence_summary: The risk assessment file's cloud-storage 'last modified' timestamp is 3 months ago, but that reflects a formatting cleanup pass; the document's own cover page and completion sign-off are dated 14 months ago with no re-performance since.
reasoning: A file's last-modified metadata is not proof of when the assessment was actually performed. The document's own stated completion date controls, and here it shows the assessment is stale beyond the 12-month window.

evidence_summary: The risk assessment has no ePHI narrative section, but its own asset and threat table flags the production database, the transcription pipeline, and the EHR integration as PHI systems and ties threats to each.
reasoning: PHI-flagged rows inside the assessment's own asset and flow inventory are the identification. A dedicated ePHI narrative section is not required when the assessment names the specific systems and ties analysis to them.

evidence_summary: The risk assessment discusses threats to 'customer data' generically. A separate asset inventory flags the ePHI systems, but the assessment never references it or distinguishes ePHI anywhere.
reasoning: The identification must live in the risk assessment itself. A generic assessment cannot borrow specificity from a separate inventory it never references, because the analysis then never actually reached the ePHI systems.

evidence_summary: The risk register itself has a 'Mapped Control(s)' column populated for every risk row, rather than a separate standalone risk-to-control matrix document.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the pass criteria accept a risk register with control-reference columns as an explicit alternative to a separate matrix. A single combined document satisfies the attribute.

evidence_summary: The one risk rated 'Elevated' in the register (the entity's top severity label, above 'Moderate' and 'Low') has a mapped control; the register simply doesn't use the literal words 'high' or 'critical' as labels.
reasoning: No over-literalism: judge the entity's own top-severity tier against the attribute's intent rather than requiring the exact words 'high' or 'critical.' The highest-rated risk here has a control mapped, satisfying the requirement.

evidence_summary: The risk-to-control mapping matrix has a control reference filled in on every one of its 14 rows. The risk register it draws from carries 17 risks, of which 5 are rated high; two of those high risks, added at the March review, do not appear in the matrix at all.
reasoning: Coverage is measured against the population of risks, not against the rows of the mapping document. A matrix in which every listed risk has a control still fails this attribute when high-rated risks from the register never made it into the matrix, because the criterion counts high or critical risks with no mapped control, and here there are two.

evidence_summary: ITGC documentation has clearly labeled sections for 'Logical Access' and 'Change Management,' and system-operations controls (monitoring, backup, incident handling) appear under a section titled 'Infrastructure Operations.'
reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute requires the three control domains to be covered, not that a section be titled exactly 'system operations.' Content under an equivalent heading satisfies the requirement.

evidence_summary: An architecture document contains a narrative paragraph explaining that access reviews depend on the identity provider and that the deploy pipeline depends on the source-control platform, rather than presenting this as a formatted dependency table.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute asks whether key business-process-to-technology dependencies are documented, not that they appear in table form. A clear narrative description of the same dependencies satisfies the requirement.

evidence_summary: Identity provider user-list export screenshot shows all 12 employees with individually named accounts (first.last@company.com); no column explicitly labeled 'shared: no'.
reasoning: Judge what the evidence shows, not how it is labeled. A live system export listing only individually named accounts plainly demonstrates no shared or generic logins exist, even without an explicit 'unique' field itemized.

evidence_summary: A client-typed onboarding spreadsheet includes a note 'all user accounts are unique, no shared logins' but no identity provider export or screenshot is attached.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof. This is a config claim about live accounts and needs an actual identity provider export or screenshot, not a self-reported assertion.

evidence_summary: Screenshot of the production application's login page shows email and password fields required before the dashboard loads; the screenshot does not also show an MFA prompt.
reasoning: Never import a neighbor attribute's requirement into this one. This attribute only requires that authentication is required before access is granted; MFA strength is tested separately under the MFA control, so its absence from this screenshot is not a failure here.

evidence_summary: During a walkthrough call, the founder states 'our app always requires login, there's no way to skip it' but no screenshot or configuration export is provided.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. A claim about system behavior needs a captured screenshot or config export showing the actual login enforcement, not a spoken assurance.

evidence_summary: A two-person company's identity provider policy enforces MFA uniformly across all systems, production and non-production alike, with no separate lower-tier policy defined.
reasoning: The 'same minimum regardless of sensitivity' fail condition targets a uniformly WEAK floor that leaves a sensitive system underprotected, not a uniformly STRONG one. Applying MFA everywhere is the strongest bar applied universally, so no higher-sensitivity system is weaker than a lower one and the control's intent is fully met.

evidence_summary: An internal architecture diagram document states 'production requires MFA, staging requires password only,' but no identity provider configuration screenshot or export corroborates the claim.
reasoning: A client-authored document is not system proof. A claim about authentication configuration by system tier requires an actual configuration export or screenshot, not a diagram description.

evidence_summary: A standalone break-glass AWS root account is documented in the security register with justification: emergency-use only, MFA-protected, credentials in a sealed vault, access reviewed quarterly.
reasoning: Compensating controls and documented justification are a legitimate pass path, not a demand that the standalone account be eliminated. A real, verifiable, documented basis for the account (restricted use, MFA, periodic review) satisfies the requirement.

evidence_summary: The IT admin states in a call that 'we don't have any standalone or local accounts outside the identity provider' but no actual account inventory or list is produced as evidence.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. Even a claim of zero standalone accounts needs an affirmative, produced list (even an empty one) to substantiate the assertion.

evidence_summary: The company is fully cloud-SaaS with no VPN or remote network access layer at all; there is no VPN configuration screenshot in the evidence set.
reasoning: Structural absence of the underlying capability is a pass path stated directly in the criteria, not a missing artifact. No VPN/remote access capability means the attribute passes by default rather than failing for lack of a VPN screenshot.

evidence_summary: A network architecture document lists 'VPN access requires MFA' as a bullet point, but no actual VPN provider configuration export or screenshot is attached.
reasoning: A client-authored document is not system proof. A configuration claim about MFA enforcement on remote access needs a captured export or screenshot from the VPN or remote-access provider itself.

evidence_summary: The onboarding checklist document details provisioning steps for new hires and role changes, and states 'the same process applies to all personnel, including contractors,' without a separate contractor-specific section.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a live document substantively covering contractors through general personnel language passes even without a separately itemized contractor section.

evidence_summary: The access management policy states 'manager sign-off is required before any account is created' rather than using the literal word 'authorization.'
reasoning: No over-literalism: substantively equivalent language requiring pre-provisioning approval satisfies the attribute even without the exact word 'authorization.'

evidence_summary: The most recent new-hire ticket contains a request comment from HR and a timestamped reply from the manager reading 'approved, please provision,' both inside the same ticket thread rather than as separate record types.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a timestamped approval comment within the same ticket thread is a legitimate documented approval, and the attribute does not require request and approval to live in separate record types.

evidence_summary: A provisioning ticket for AWS console access lists the same username in both the requester field and the approver field.
reasoning: An approval step existing is not the same as an authorized approval. The criteria require approval from a manager or system owner distinct from the requester, and a matching requester and approver identity is self-approval, which is a gap regardless of the presence of an approval field.

evidence_summary: The access comparison record shows the new hire received the requested engineering role plus a standard company-wide read-only baseline group that is automatically applied to every employee account.
reasoning: No over-literalism: an automatically applied, organization-wide baseline group is not additional access beyond the request in substance, and should not be treated as scope creep just because it was not separately itemized in the request.

evidence_summary: The approved access request for a new support hire specifies the helpdesk tool and read-only access to the booking console. The identity provider export for that user shows both of those, plus membership in the 'billing-admin' group granted the same afternoon. No request or approval mentions billing.
reasoning: Matching runs in both directions, so access present in the system but absent from the approved request fails this attribute just as squarely as access that was requested and never granted. The criteria call out additional roles beyond what was requested, and an unrequested admin group is the case they exist for.

evidence_summary: The offboarding checklist instructs staff to 'revoke all system access per the current access inventory' rather than naming each of the company's 15 in-scope systems individually.
reasoning: No over-literalism: referencing the maintained access inventory as the authoritative source for revocation substantively covers all in-scope systems without re-listing each one in the checklist itself.

evidence_summary: The offboarding policy states access must be removed 'by end of business day on the termination date' rather than using the phrase '24 hours.'
reasoning: No over-literalism: 'end of business day' is a specific, defined maximum timeframe that satisfies the requirement just as well as an hour-count phrasing.

evidence_summary: The company's offboarding policy defines a 3-business-day removal window; the most recent termination shows the identity provider account disabled 2 business days after the HR termination date.
reasoning: Judge against the entity's own documented timeframe, not an assumed industry norm such as same-day removal. Removal within the client's defined 3-business-day window satisfies the attribute even though it is not instantaneous.

evidence_summary: The termination verification record confirms the identity provider account was disabled, but no check is documented for the same individual's cloud console, code repository, or business application access.
reasoning: Partial-system evidence should not be credited as complete coverage. The criteria require zero active accounts across all in-scope systems, and confirming only the identity provider leaves cloud consoles, code repos, and business apps unverified, which is a gap in coverage, not a pass.

evidence_summary: The offboarding record shows timestamps for identity provider disablement and systems access revocation, but no timestamp for a peripheral checklist line item like laptop return.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: the criteria only require timestamps for the minimum key deprovisioning steps, IdP disable and systems access revocation, both of which are present; a missing timestamp on an unrelated checklist item like equipment return is outside this attribute's scope.

evidence_summary: The access review requirement appears as a clause inside the company's combined 'Access Control and Onboarding/Offboarding Policy' rather than in a standalone 'Access Review Policy,' stating management reviews access quarterly.
reasoning: No over-literalism: judge the substance of what the policy requires, not the document title or section heading it lives under. The clause plainly requires periodic reviews by management with a stated quarterly frequency, which is exactly what the attribute tests, so it passes regardless of which policy file contains it.

evidence_summary: The access review scope checklist lists 'cloud infrastructure' and 'core SaaS tools' as umbrella categories covering AWS, GCP, and the HR system, rather than naming each system individually.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a category umbrella that demonstrably includes every in-scope system satisfies the attribute even without itemizing each system by name. Confirm the umbrella actually maps to the full in-scope list before failing on formatting alone.

evidence_summary: The most recent access review is logged as a dated, completed task in the team's shared Notion tracker rather than in a dedicated access-review tool, showing the review was performed on the quarterly schedule.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and timing of the review, not the hygiene or format of the tool used to log it. A dated record in an ordinary task tracker is still a dated record if it shows the review occurred on schedule.

evidence_summary: The reviewer states in an interview note that 'all systems were checked' during the last access review, but the review record itself only lists AWS and GitHub with no mention of the company's newly adopted Slack workspace.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never a substitute for the review record itself. The written record must enumerate the systems reviewed, and an in-scope system absent from that record is a real coverage gap even if someone claims otherwise verbally.

evidence_summary: The review record lists the reviewer as 'Admin User' for the production database review, and the AI treats any account with 'Admin' in its name as evidence the system owner performed the review.
reasoning: Never accept a generic account label at face value without confirming it maps to the actual named system owner. A shared or generic admin account name is not proof that the designated owner performed the review versus a delegate or the account holder reviewing their own access.

evidence_summary: A flagged over-permissioned account from the last review was removed the same week, evidenced only by a timestamped Slack message from the reviewer confirming the access was revoked, with no formal ticketing system in use.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a timestamped message confirming remediation is sufficient proof of timely action for a small team without a formal ticketing system. Demanding a specific ticket format when the substance (dated removal within the defined timeframe) is clearly shown is over-literal.

evidence_summary: An Okta screenshot shows named groups (Engineering, Finance, Admin) each with a description field listing their associated permissions, but there is no separate written 'role definitions' document.
reasoning: Live system evidence showing defined roles and their permissions passes even without a companion policy document. The identity provider's own configuration is system evidence of documented roles regardless of whether a redundant document also exists.

evidence_summary: A submitted 'Future Access Model' project document lists proposed roles and permissions but is marked 'DRAFT - pending implementation' with several TODO placeholders and no adoption date.
reasoning: A draft or project document is not an adopted configuration. Placeholder text and an explicit draft banner mean the roles described are not yet in force, so this fails until the roles are shown as actually implemented in the system.

evidence_summary: An Okta export shows the large majority of employees assigned access via groups, with two long-term contractors holding individual app grants that each have a documented business justification note attached.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: the pass criteria explicitly tolerate a minority of individual grants when documented with justification, so a small number of justified exceptions is not a structural failure. Only access primarily assigned through ungoverned individual grants should fail this attribute.

evidence_summary: A client-authored spreadsheet states '95% of access is assigned through groups' with no accompanying identity-provider export or screenshot to substantiate the figure.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. This attribute tests actual IdP assignment structure, which requires a system export or screenshot corroborating the stated percentage, not a self-reported figure.

evidence_summary: A sampled DevOps engineer holds both AWS infrastructure-admin access and read-only billing console access; the job description confirms cost-monitoring duties as part of the role.
reasoning: No over-literalism: an access grant that falls outside the narrowest reading of a job title still aligns with job function when the job description documents the underlying duty. Verify against the actual documented responsibilities before flagging a mismatch.

evidence_summary: A live screenshot of the AWS IAM console listing all admin-role users was submitted under a generic file name and initially tagged as a miscellaneous document rather than as system evidence.
reasoning: Live system screenshots are system evidence regardless of how they were labeled at submission. Judge the content of the corpus, not the filename or tag it arrived with, before concluding the inventory is missing.

evidence_summary: A founder-typed spreadsheet lists the names of people believed to have admin access to AWS and GitHub, with no accompanying console export or API pull from either system.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a privileged-user inventory. The claim requires an actual export or live capture from each in-scope system, not a list typed from memory.

evidence_summary: A privileged access grant is authorized via a timestamped Slack message from the engineering manager approving admin access for a specific incident-response need, with no formal ticketing system in place.
reasoning: No over-literalism: an informal but verifiable, timestamped approval record satisfies the authorization requirement for a small team without a ticketing system. The substance is a documented approval carrying a business justification, which is what the attribute tests.

evidence_summary: During the walkthrough interview the IT lead states 'we always approve admin access before granting it,' but no approval record, ticket, or email is provided for any of the sampled privileged users.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never a substitute for documented authorization. Each privileged user needs an actual retrievable authorization artifact, not a general assurance given in conversation.

evidence_summary: A screenshot shows CloudTrail enabled at the AWS Organizations management account as an org-wide trail, which by design also logs activity in every member account, but no per-member-account screenshot was separately captured.
reasoning: No over-literalism: an organization-wide trail configured at the management account level demonstrably covers every member account by design, so a live capture proving that structure passes without a redundant per-account screenshot.

evidence_summary: The evidence submitted is a page from the cloud provider's public documentation describing that CloudTrail 'can log all account activity,' with no screenshot of this organization's own trail configuration.
reasoning: A provider's documentation page is not this organization's configuration. The attribute requires proof that logging is actually enabled in this entity's own environment, not a description of the feature's general availability.

evidence_summary: A live export from the secrets manager shows each service account's resource tags populated with 'Owner' and 'Purpose' fields, but there is no separate formal service-account registry document.
reasoning: Live system evidence showing the required fields passes even without a redundant standalone document. The secrets manager's own tagging is system evidence of ownership and purpose regardless of format.

evidence_summary: A founder-typed spreadsheet lists each service account with an owner name and purpose description, with no corresponding export from the secrets manager or cloud console to confirm the accounts or fields exist there.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. The owner and purpose fields need to be corroborated by an actual system export, not asserted in a self-made document.

evidence_summary: A secrets manager screenshot shows automatic rotation configured with a rotation Lambda attached to each service credential, but does not show a completed rotation event log or 'last rotated' timestamp.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: this attribute passes on automatic rotation being enabled in configuration, not on a rotation having already executed, which belongs to operating-effectiveness testing elsewhere. A screenshot of the rotation configuration being enabled is sufficient at the design stage.

evidence_summary: During the interview the founder states 'we rotate all service credentials every quarter,' but no secrets manager configuration screenshot or rotation policy setting was provided.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config evidence. The rotation schedule or automatic rotation setting must be shown in the actual system configuration or in dated manual rotation records, not asserted verbally.

evidence_summary: The service account review is recorded as a distinct, separately-labeled tab within the same quarterly access-review spreadsheet, showing last-used dates and two disabled unused accounts.
reasoning: No over-literalism: 'separate from user access reviews' means functionally distinct in scope and method, not housed in an entirely different document or tool. A clearly delineated section that independently evaluates service accounts by last-used date and disables unused ones satisfies the requirement.

evidence_summary: Engineering maintains a living architecture page in the team wiki that diagrams the VPCs, subnets, and data flow between services, reviewed and updated four months ago; there is no separate exported diagram file.
reasoning: A network architecture document can take any durable form (wiki page, diagram tool, slide) as long as it shows environments, segments, and connectivity and was reviewed within 24 months; don't demand a specific file format. The wiki page is current and complete on substance.

evidence_summary: An engineer captured a live screenshot of the cloud console showing separate AWS accounts for production and staging, submitted under a generic filename with no explicit lane tag at upload time.
reasoning: Live system screenshots are system evidence regardless of how they were labeled at submission; judge what the capture shows, not its filename or tag. A plainly separate account structure between prod and staging satisfies isolation.

evidence_summary: The client submitted a spreadsheet they typed themselves listing production and staging VPC IDs, with no accompanying console capture or export.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. Without a captured export or corroborating system view, the isolation claim is unverified and should be a gap pending an actual console screenshot or export.

evidence_summary: A security group export shows explicit allow rules scoped to specific ports between segments (app tier to database on 5432 only), with no allow-all entries anywhere, but no written narrative explains each rule's rationale.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a live export plainly showing scoped, non-allow-all rules passes even without an accompanying narrative explaining least-privilege intent. The rules themselves demonstrate the control.

evidence_summary: An engineer stated on a call that production and staging don't share any open network rules, but no security group or firewall export was provided.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The segmentation claim needs an actual rules export or screenshot before it can pass.

evidence_summary: A three-person startup runs on a managed hosting platform behind a CDN provider; a screenshot shows the CDN's proxy/WAF toggle enabled on the production domain, with no dedicated firewall appliance in place.
reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage: a cloud-native boundary mechanism like a managed WAF/proxy satisfies this attribute at this scale. The pass should state explicitly that it rests on the compensating cloud-native control.

evidence_summary: The evidence submitted was a screenshot of the CDN provider's public marketing page describing its WAF product, not a screenshot of the client's own zone or domain settings.
reasoning: A provider's marketing or trust page is not this org's configuration. The entity must show its own dashboard or zone settings with the mechanism actually enabled for its domain.

evidence_summary: A firewall export shows exactly two inbound rules: port 443 open to all, and port 80 redirecting to 443; no other ports appear anywhere in the rule set.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a fully captured rule set with only public web ports open is itself proof that nothing else is exposed. Don't demand a rule explicitly stating that admin ports are closed when the complete export shows none exist.

evidence_summary: The client typed a note stating that SSH access is restricted to the office IP address; no firewall or security group export was attached.
reasoning: A client-authored note is not system proof. A port-restriction claim needs an actual firewall or security-group export or console screenshot.

evidence_summary: Engineering maintains an internal wiki page listing every public subdomain and its purpose, last reviewed and updated within the quarter.
reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: a maintained internal list is the proportional artifact for this attribute at this company's size. Existence and currency of the inventory is what's tested, not the specific tool used to produce it.

evidence_summary: The hosting provider's public status page, listing the provider's own infrastructure regions, was submitted as the entity's external access point inventory.
reasoning: A provider's infrastructure page is not this org's configuration. The entity needs its own list of its domains, endpoints, and IP addresses, not the vendor's general infrastructure description.

evidence_summary: The team uses a device-based zero-trust access tool gated by SSO and MFA with encrypted tunnels, instead of a traditional VPN client.
reasoning: Compensating controls are legitimate at design stage: a zero-trust access tool enforcing MFA and encryption is equivalent to a VPN for this attribute. State the compensating basis explicitly when passing.

evidence_summary: The IT admin said on a call that remote access requires MFA, but no VPN or zero-trust configuration screenshot or export was submitted.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The MFA-and-encryption claim needs an actual configuration capture showing both requirements enforced.

evidence_summary: The four-person company works out of a shared coworking space with no dedicated leased facility; the coworking operator's badge system gates entry to the building and floor, documented as the client's physical access control.
reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: for a company with no facility of its own, a shared building's badge-gated access is the proportional control. State the compensating basis explicitly when passing.

evidence_summary: The office manager said in an interview that a badge is required to enter the building, with no badge system export, access request form, or building management confirmation provided.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence. A physical access authorization claim needs a badge system screenshot/export or an access request form on file.

evidence_summary: The office has one shared key-card reader for the floor; the server closet uses a separate physical lock with keys held only by the two engineers, documented in a short internal access note.
reasoning: Proportional compensating control: a distinct physical lock restricted to a named subset of personnel satisfies additional access controls beyond general facility access, even without a second badge reader.

evidence_summary: The facilities lead said restricted areas have extra security without describing what it is, and no documentation or photo of the actual control was provided.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence. The claim needs a description or capture of the actual additional control (lock type, reader, biometric) in place.

evidence_summary: The offboarding checklist has a line item for badge return and access deactivation, and the two departures logged this quarter both show the box checked with a date, though the checklist template itself hasn't been reformatted in over a year.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and use of the process, not the hygiene of its paperwork. A used, dated checklist entry evidencing revocation is sufficient even if the template is old.

evidence_summary: The small office keeps a paper sign-in sheet at the front desk recording visitor name, date, and who they were meeting; it is not a digital visitor-management system.
reasoning: Proportional form passes: the attribute tests that visitors are identified and logged, not that a specific software system is used. A maintained paper log with name, date, and host satisfies the control.

evidence_summary: Eight months ago the office manager emailed IT confirming who currently holds a badge and flagging two people to remove; the note isn't titled a physical access review and uses no formal template.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on substance, not on label or template. A dated review of who holds access with documented follow-up action satisfies the annual review requirement even without a dedicated review document.

evidence_summary: A cloud console screenshot shows encryption enabled on the production database instance and on the storage bucket's default encryption setting, but the capture doesn't separately name the algorithm as AES-256 even though that is the service's documented default.
reasoning: No over-literalism: when a managed service's encryption toggle is enabled and its documented default algorithm meets or exceeds the minimum, the capture doesn't need to spell out the algorithm name to pass.

evidence_summary: The client wrote in a spreadsheet that all databases are encrypted at rest, with no console screenshot or export showing the actual encryption settings.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. The encryption-at-rest claim needs an actual console capture or export.

evidence_summary: A TLS scan of the production API endpoint shows only TLS 1.2 and 1.3 as supported protocols; the report doesn't include a separate line explicitly stating SSLv3 is disabled.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a scan listing only modern TLS versions as supported IS proof that older protocols are disabled; absence of an explicit negative line item is not a gap.

evidence_summary: Engineering said in a standup that only modern TLS versions are allowed, with no scan report, load balancer configuration, or endpoint capture submitted.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The TLS-version claim needs an actual scan output or configuration export.

evidence_summary: The transit-side TLS scan confirms compliant key exchange and cipher suites, but doesn't separately show a database encryption key length, which is covered by a different attribute's own evidence.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: don't import a neighboring attribute's evidence requirement into this one. If the algorithms and key lengths shown for this attribute's scope meet the standard, that is sufficient.

evidence_summary: A security questionnaire response stated the company uses strong encryption and modern key lengths, with no actual configuration or scan output attached.
reasoning: Written self-attestation without a capture is not configuration evidence. The algorithm and key-length claim needs an actual scan or configuration export.

evidence_summary: A code repository search for common secret patterns shows zero hits, and a separate secrets-manager dashboard screenshot shows the production signing key stored there; the two captures come from different tools rather than one unified report.
reasoning: Judge the substance across the corpus, not whether it arrives in one unified report. A clean code-scan capture plus a secrets-manager capture together satisfy the attribute.

evidence_summary: The engineering lead said on a call that keys are never hardcoded, with no code scan results or secrets manager configuration provided.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence. The no-plaintext-keys claim needs an actual code scan output or secrets manager configuration capture.

evidence_summary: A KMS console screenshot shows automatic key rotation toggled on for the production key; there is no separate rotation history log showing a completed rotation event yet.
reasoning: Read the pass criteria precisely: automatic rotation enabled is an independent, sufficient pass path. Don't additionally demand a manual rotation history log when auto-rotation is on.

evidence_summary: An admin said verbally that keys are rotated every year, with no KMS configuration screenshot or rotation log provided.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The rotation claim needs an actual KMS config screenshot or a dated rotation log.

evidence_summary: The company's asset handling policy has a short paragraph stating laptops are wiped via full-disk encryption key destruction before being recycled through a certified e-waste vendor; there are no other asset types since the company is fully cloud-based with no on-prem servers.
reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: the procedure must be proportional to the entity's actual asset footprint. A short but concrete description covering the only asset type in use satisfies the attribute.

evidence_summary: No laptops or hardware were disposed of during the period; the client has a written disposal procedure on file but no disposal events occurred to test against it.
reasoning: Absence of disposal activity is a pass-by-default condition under this attribute's own criteria, not a gap. An AI that treats nothing-to-sample as an automatic fail is over-conservative; verify there truly were no disposals before failing.

evidence_summary: The client stated no assets were disposed of during the period, so no destruction certificates or wipe logs were provided. The asset inventory submitted for the asset control shows six laptops moved to status 'retired' with retirement dates inside the period, plus one line noting a hardware return to the leasing vendor.
reasoning: A pass by default for a non-occurrence has to be corroborated by the record, never accepted on assertion alone. The entity's own inventory shows disposals inside the period, so the no-disposals branch of the criteria does not apply, and the absence of any wipe log, certificate, or vendor receipt for those six assets is a gap.

evidence_summary: The most recent disposal record shows the asset tag, disposal date, and wipe method used, but the entry lives in a shared internal document rather than a dedicated disposal-log tool.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on substance, not on the tool that holds it. A shared document entry that includes asset identifier, date, and method satisfies the documentation requirement regardless of what software it's kept in.

evidence_summary: Retention periods for customer data appear in the main security policy, and retention periods for employee data and system logs appear in a separate HR data-handling addendum; no single consolidated schedule exists.
