reasoning: The substance of a defined retention schedule can live across more than one document as long as each required category is covered with defined periods. Customer, employee, and log retention periods are all present and were reviewed together, so splitting them across a security policy and an HR addendum still satisfies the attribute.

evidence_summary: A clean, professional-looking retention schedule defines specific periods for every data category, but has no column or notes citing any legal, regulatory, or contractual basis for those periods.
reasoning: This attribute adds a distinct requirement beyond a schedule existing: each retention period needs a documented legal, regulatory, or contractual basis. Reasonable-looking periods with no basis column at all satisfy the neighbor attribute (schedule defined) but fail this one, which demands the justification be documented.

evidence_summary: One MDM screenshot shows FileVault enabled on all laptops and a second screenshot from the same console shows USB storage restricted, taken moments apart during the same review session.
reasoning: Live system evidence counts regardless of whether every sub-clause is captured in a single screenshot. The same console session plainly shows both endpoint encryption and removable-media restriction, so two screenshots from one live source are together sufficient system proof.

evidence_summary: An engineer states in a review call that the team tells new hires verbally not to plug in personal USB drives, but no MDM configuration, policy document, or acceptable-use text was found.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. A spoken practice with no MDM enforcement and no written policy leaves removable media effectively unrestricted, which is the failure condition for this attribute.

evidence_summary: An S3 lifecycle policy document describes automatic deletion of customer data after the retention window, configured last quarter; the company has not yet had a case where the window actually elapsed and data was purged.
reasoning: A process-plus-enforcement attribute passes on a real, configured enforcement mechanism, not on a history of executions that have not yet come due. An automated lifecycle policy that is actually configured and would fire on schedule satisfies the enforcement requirement even with no purge event to point to yet.

evidence_summary: The retention policy describes deletion at the end of each retention period clearly and by data category. The cloud console shows no lifecycle rules on the buckets holding the archived permit files, no scheduled deletion job exists, and no owner is named for carrying it out manually.
reasoning: This attribute requires the process and an enforcement mechanism behind it, so a policy describing deletion with nothing arranged to perform it fails. A manual route can satisfy the enforcement half, but only with a named owner and evidence it happens, and neither is present here.

evidence_summary: The data handling policy prohibits storing production data, including ePHI, on laptops and removable media, with no exceptions.
reasoning: Prohibition is one of the two accepted policy positions. An inventory of local ePHI storage is only required when such storage is permitted, so failing a prohibition policy for lacking one is wrong.

evidence_summary: The acceptable use policy tells staff to 'handle patient data with care' and to 'avoid keeping files locally where possible'. No definite position on local ePHI storage appears anywhere.
reasoning: An exhortation to be careful is not a policy position. The policy must either prohibit local ePHI storage or set the inventory, encryption, and backup requirements for it; 'avoid where possible' does neither.

evidence_summary: An EDR console export shows 11 of 12 managed devices covered; the twelfth is a laptop already wiped and removed from the active roster per a closed IT offboarding ticket dated before the test date.
reasoning: Coverage is measured against the true current managed population, not a stale device count. A laptop confirmed decommissioned and removed from service is no longer a managed endpoint, so coverage of the actual current fleet is 100 percent and passes.

evidence_summary: The founder states in the interview that 'all our laptops have antivirus installed' but no MDM or EDR console export, device list, or screenshot was provided to confirm deployment.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. A spoken assurance about endpoint coverage with no system export to inspect cannot establish the 100 percent deployment this attribute requires.

evidence_summary: An MDM console screenshot shows an aggregate compliance tile reading '8/8 devices, 100% FileVault enabled' rather than a row-by-row per-device listing.
reasoning: A live console's own aggregate compliance figure is system evidence of the substance required, full disk encryption enforced across the fleet. An itemized per-device row is not required when the console itself reports 100 percent enforced.

evidence_summary: The written security policy states 'FileVault is required on all company laptops,' but no MDM query, console screenshot, or endpoint export confirming the actual enforced state was provided.
reasoning: A policy statement is not proof of the live configuration it describes. This attribute requires a system capture showing encryption is actually enforced, so a written requirement alone gaps pending real config evidence.

evidence_summary: MDM enforces a 10-minute screen lock timeout on company-owned devices; two contractors use personal BYOD laptops outside MDM enrollment, but a documented BYOD policy requires the same timeout and each contractor has signed an acceptable-use agreement confirming it.
reasoning: A compensating control is a legitimate pass path when the basis is real and documented. A signed BYOD policy enforcing the equivalent idle timeout stands in for direct MDM enforcement on devices outside the platform's reach, so this passes on that documented compensating basis.

evidence_summary: An onboarding checklist has a manually checked box next to 'enable screen lock' for each new hire, with no MDM policy or system query confirming the actual setting on any device.
reasoning: A self-attestation checklist is not configuration evidence. Ticking a box during onboarding proves an instruction was given, not that the setting is actually enforced on the device, so it gaps absent a system-level confirmation.

evidence_summary: MDM enforces automatic OS updates, but third-party application updates are handled through a documented monthly patch cadence run manually by IT rather than an automated tool.
reasoning: Read the full pass criteria before failing: it explicitly accepts a managed patch process with a defined cadence as an alternative to automation. Automated OS updates alongside a documented, enforced monthly third-party patching routine satisfies the attribute rather than failing for not being fully automatic.

evidence_summary: An internal wiki page recommends 'employees should turn on automatic updates,' but no MDM policy, script, or device query confirms the setting is actually enforced anywhere.
reasoning: An aspirational recommendation is not an adopted, enforced control. A suggestion with no enforcement mechanism or verification leaves the actual patch state unknown, so it gaps pending real enforcement evidence.

evidence_summary: An EDR console export covering the full period shows zero detected threats or alerts; no investigation or remediation records exist because nothing was ever flagged.
reasoning: Read the default-pass clause before failing: the attribute explicitly passes when no threats were detected as of the test date. An empty alert log with no incidents to investigate is a pass, not a missing-evidence gap.

evidence_summary: A CI/CD pipeline settings screenshot shows only two named accounts hold deploy permission to production; no separate raw IAM policy JSON export was provided alongside it.
reasoning: A live pipeline permissions screen plainly showing restricted deploy access is system evidence of the control. A second export format is not required when the substance, that only authorized accounts can deploy, is already visible.

evidence_summary: The engineering handbook states 'only admins can deploy to production,' but no CI/CD permissions export, IAM policy, or console screenshot was provided to confirm the actual access configuration.
reasoning: A written policy statement is not proof of the live access configuration it describes. Without a system export showing who can actually deploy, this gaps pending real configuration evidence.

evidence_summary: A system-pulled admin roster shows 3 of 8 engineers hold production admin rights (about 38 percent), each with a documented business justification for the access.
reasoning: The 30 percent admin ratio is a review trigger, not an automatic fail: the criteria call for flagging ratios above it for CPA attention. A documented, justified admin list above the threshold passes with a note for reviewer attention rather than gapping.

evidence_summary: The founder compiles a list of production admins from memory and email searches rather than pulling it from the actual IAM console or access management system.
reasoning: A client-authored recollection is not system proof of who holds admin access. An admin list is a system-state claim that needs to come from an actual access management export, not a founder's memory, so it gaps pending a real roster.

evidence_summary: The company has no MDM platform, but its acceptable-use policy explicitly prohibits use of removable media without a documented exception process, signed by all employees.
reasoning: A governing policy is an explicit alternative pass path here, not just technical MDM enforcement. A clear, signed acceptable-use restriction on removable media satisfies the attribute, so it passes rather than gapping for lacking an MDM setting.

evidence_summary: An employee mentions in an interview that 'nobody really uses USB drives here,' with no MDM restriction and no written policy addressing removable media at all.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration or policy evidence. An informal spoken habit with neither a technical restriction nor a governing policy leaves removable media ungoverned, which is the failure condition.

evidence_summary: The CI/CD pipeline requires a passing peer-reviewed pull request and green automated checks before any merge to the branch that triggers a production deploy; there is no separate manual change-ticket system.
reasoning: A git-based review-and-checks gate that actually blocks unreviewed deploys IS the change management process this attribute asks for. It embeds review, approval, and testing, so it passes even without a standalone ticketing tool layered on top.

evidence_summary: A live screenshot of the vulnerability scanner's target configuration shows every in-scope repository and cloud account listed, but it was tagged as a plain screenshot rather than an auto-pulled export.
reasoning: Live system screenshots are system evidence regardless of how they were labeled at submission, so judge what the capture shows, not its lane tag. The scan target list plainly covers every in-scope system, satisfying the attribute.

evidence_summary: A client-authored spreadsheet titled 'systems we scan' lists all in-scope assets, but no screenshot or export from the scanning tool itself was provided.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim; it needs provenance from the tool itself or corroboration against a system view. Without a scanner-side capture, coverage cannot be verified.

evidence_summary: The scan report groups findings using CVSS numeric score bands (9.0-10.0, 7.0-8.9, 4.0-6.9, 0.1-3.9) with color coding instead of the literal words critical/high/medium/low.
reasoning: Do not demand the literal words when the evidence plainly conveys the same severity tiers; a live capture showing the substance passes even if sub-clauses are not itemized identically. The CVSS bands map directly onto the four required severity levels.

evidence_summary: No significant infrastructure changes occurred during the audit period, and no scan-to-change correlation record was submitted.
reasoning: Apply the attribute's own na/default-pass condition before failing for missing evidence; when no significant changes occurred, the attribute passes by default rather than requiring a correlation record that has nothing to correlate against.

evidence_summary: The vulnerability scanner runs continuous background scanning (re-scans on every dependency push) rather than producing discrete periodic scan reports at a fixed interval.
reasoning: Continuous scanning is a legitimate compensating design for a discrete-frequency requirement, provided the basis is real and verifiable; continuous coverage necessarily satisfies any periodic interval and should not be failed for lacking discrete report dates.

evidence_summary: An internal onboarding doc states 'we scan weekly' but no scan history, dashboard export, or tool configuration screenshot was submitted to verify actual scan cadence.
reasoning: A config/system-state claim needs provenance or corroboration from the system itself, not a client assertion. A written statement of intended cadence does not prove the scanner actually ran at that frequency.

evidence_summary: No critical or high severity findings were identified in any scan run during the audit period, and no remediation record was submitted.
reasoning: Apply the attribute's own na/default-pass condition before failing for missing remediation records; with zero critical/high findings in the period, the attribute passes by default rather than requiring evidence of remediation that never needed to happen.

evidence_summary: The scanner dashboard shows the most recent critical finding, a remote code execution issue on the routing API host, marked resolved with a fix date 6 days after detection, inside the entity's 14 day critical SLA. The scan output exported the same week still lists that CVE on that host at the same severity.
reasoning: A remediation record is a claim about system state and has to agree with the system, so a finding marked resolved while the scanner still reports it is unremediated. Where a tracker and the live scan disagree the scan governs, since closing a ticket is an action taken in the tracker and not on the host.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the penetration testing vendor's client portal shows the completed engagement with a test-completion date nine months ago, but the report PDF itself was not attached.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing; a vendor portal capture showing the completed test date is system evidence of the same fact the report would state and should be judged on what it shows, not on which specific artifact format was uploaded.

evidence_summary: The 'penetration test' was performed and self-attested by the same two-person engineering team that built and maintains the production systems being tested, with no external firm or separated internal function involved.
reasoning: A test is not independent merely because a report exists; the pass criteria explicitly fail self-performed testing by the team responsible for the systems tested. No compensating basis was documented for treating this internal self-test as independent.

evidence_summary: The penetration test report's scope section describes testing 'the production web application and its API' broadly, without separately naming every subdomain or microservice that falls under that application.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a scope description that substantively covers the in-scope systems passes even without itemizing every sub-asset by name, so long as the named scope plainly encompasses them.

evidence_summary: Each finding in the report carries a color-coded icon (red/orange/yellow/blue) and a numeric CVSS score in place of the words critical/high/medium/low.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a consistent color and score scheme that maps directly to severity tiers conveys the same information as the named labels and satisfies the attribute.

evidence_summary: The penetration test identified no critical or high severity findings, only a handful of informational observations, and no remediation record was submitted for those.
reasoning: Apply the attribute's own na/default-pass condition before failing for missing remediation evidence; with no critical or high findings, the attribute passes by default.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the AWS Organizations CloudTrail console shows a single organization-level trail applied to all member accounts, rather than a separately configured trail shown for each individual account.
reasoning: No over-literalism: an organization-level trail that applies to every member account by design covers all in-scope systems without needing a repeated per-account capture.

evidence_summary: An internal infrastructure spreadsheet lists 'logging: enabled' next to every server and service, but no CloudTrail, cloud console, or logging-platform screenshot was submitted.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim; the actual logging platform or cloud console needs to be captured to verify logging is truly enabled.

evidence_summary: The log platform's enabled sources are named 'sign-in events,' 'permission and role changes,' 'infrastructure configuration changes,' 'admin console actions,' and 'application error and exception logs' rather than the literal category labels used in the entity's policy.
reasoning: No over-literalism: differently worded log category names that map onto the same five required categories satisfy the attribute; the substance, not the label text, controls. All five required types are present here under alternative names.

evidence_summary: The evidence submitted is the cloud provider's public documentation page describing what its audit logging service is capable of capturing, rather than a screenshot of this organization's own enabled log sources.
reasoning: A provider's marketing or documentation page is not this organization's actual configuration; capability descriptions must be replaced with a capture of what this org has actually turned on.

evidence_summary: The log storage bucket's lifecycle policy screenshot shows a rule retaining objects for 400 days, phrased as an S3 lifecycle rule rather than a field explicitly labeled 'log retention.'
reasoning: No over-literalism: a lifecycle or storage rule that functionally retains the logs for the required period satisfies the attribute even if it is not labeled 'retention' in those exact words.

evidence_summary: The engineering lead told the CPA in a call that 'logs are kept for at least a year,' but no retention configuration screenshot or export was provided.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config evidence; a stated retention period must be verified against an actual configuration screen or export.

evidence_summary: The log bucket has versioning enabled, MFA-delete required, and an IAM policy restricting delete permissions to a single break-glass admin role, but there is no separately toggled 'Object Lock' or 'immutability' setting.
reasoning: A compensating combination of controls (versioning, MFA-delete, restricted delete permissions) is a legitimate pass path when the basis is real and verifiable, even without the single named immutability feature the attribute's typical evidence describes.

evidence_summary: An IT-authored access control document states 'only admins can access the logs,' but no screenshot of the actual IAM policy or log group permissions was submitted.
reasoning: A client-authored access description is not system proof; the actual permissions configuration must be captured to confirm non-admins cannot alter or delete logs.

evidence_summary: The monitoring platform has active monitors for repeated failed logins, geographically anomalous access, and unexpected infrastructure configuration drift, but they are internally labeled as 'SLO monitors' rather than 'threat alert rules.'
reasoning: No over-literalism: monitors that substantively detect the required threat scenarios satisfy the attribute regardless of the internal label used for the monitor category.

evidence_summary: A security roadmap document lists 'alerts we plan to configure next quarter' for brute force and privilege escalation, but no screenshot of currently live, configured alert rules in the monitoring platform was provided.
reasoning: A planning document is not an adopted configuration; future intent does not satisfy an attribute that requires alert rules to actually exist now.

evidence_summary: No security alerts were triggered by the monitoring platform during the audit period, and no triage or review record was submitted.
reasoning: Apply the attribute's own na/default-pass condition before failing for missing review records; with zero alerts triggered in the period, there is nothing to triage and the attribute passes by default.

evidence_summary: The IR Plan document has a single 'Response Workflow' narrative section that walks through detection, containment, and cleanup steps together as one continuous process, rather than under six separately labeled headings.
reasoning: An attribute passes when the evidence plainly shows the substance, even if sub-elements are not separately itemized under matching headings. The narrative covers all six required elements (roles, severity, containment, eradication, recovery, communication) in substance, so it passes.

evidence_summary: The incident response plan is detailed on roles and responsibilities, severity classification, containment, recovery, and communication protocols. It contains no eradication procedures; the plan moves from isolating an affected host directly to restoring service, with nothing on removing the cause from the environment.
reasoning: This attribute enumerates six required elements and a plan is judged against the list, not against how complete it feels. Eradication is a distinct phase from containment and recovery, and skipping it is how an entity restores service onto a system the intruder still holds.

evidence_summary: The IR Plan's 'Security Incident Notification' section lists who to notify, timing, and method for any incident affecting customer data, but never uses the word 'breach.'
reasoning: Judge the attribute's actual text, not stricter wording the criteria never demanded. The clause requires communication protocols and notification procedures, both present in substance under different terminology, so it passes.

evidence_summary: The IR Plan is stored as a shared document with no cover-page date, but its version history shows a substantive edit and comment resolution four months ago.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: a live system artifact like document version history is valid proof of a review date regardless of the format the pass criteria's example anticipated. The history plainly shows a review within the past 12 months.

evidence_summary: No security incidents occurred during the period. After a tabletop walkthrough, the two-person team posted a short recap in a shared chat channel noting what worked and one process change to make, but never produced a formal 'lessons learned' document.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and use of the process, not the formality of its writeup. A tabletop is an explicitly valid evaluation basis when no incidents occurred, and the recap captures lessons learned in substance.

evidence_summary: The solo founder ran an informal 45-minute walkthrough of the incident response steps with a contractor, documented in a shared doc with participants and a date, but the company never called it a 'tabletop exercise' or 'drill.'
reasoning: Judge substance over label: a documented walkthrough of IR steps with participants and a date is a training event regardless of what it is titled. For a solo/small team, this proportional form of exercise satisfies the attribute.

evidence_summary: A calendar invite exists for a tabletop exercise scheduled for next month; no exercise has actually taken place yet in the audit period.
reasoning: Scheduling an activity is not evidence the activity occurred. The attribute requires a dated record of a completed exercise with scenario documentation and results, and a future calendar invite provides neither.

evidence_summary: The breach response procedure is documented, and the company's IR tabletop scenario involved an engineer accidentally exposing a database containing customer emails, which the team walked through end to end.
reasoning: Never import a stricter requirement than the attribute text actually demands. The tabletop scenario is functionally a personal-data breach even though it was not labeled that way, so it satisfies the 'tested' requirement.

evidence_summary: No incidents occurred during the review period, and the entity has a documented containment and mitigation process in its IR plan.
reasoning: Apply the pass-by-default clause when it is written into the pass criteria. The criteria explicitly state pass by default if no incidents occurred as of the test date, so a gap verdict here ignores the attribute's own text.

evidence_summary: The single incident record in the period has a bulleted 'why this happened' section identifying a misconfigured firewall rule as the cause, but the document has no heading called 'Root Cause Analysis.'
reasoning: No over-literalism: the record identifies an underlying cause in substance, which is what the attribute tests, not the presence of a specific section title. The attribute passes.

evidence_summary: The most recent incident record, a four hour outage of the bidding service, has a populated 'root cause' field reading 'human error'. Nothing in the record identifies what action was taken, which control did not prevent it, or why it was possible.
reasoning: A populated field is not an analysis, and this attribute requires the underlying cause to be identified rather than labelled. Human error names the last person in the chain and stops exactly where the useful investigation starts, so nothing in the record could drive a corrective action.

evidence_summary: The status page for the incident shows a timestamped 'Resolved - service restored' update, but the internal incident ticket itself has no restoration note.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: a live status-page capture is valid system evidence of restoration regardless of which artifact was expected to carry it. The restoration timestamp is documented and corroborated by a system-generated record.

evidence_summary: During the interview, the founder stated that affected customers are always emailed after any incident, but no notification email, template, or send log was provided for the one qualifying incident in the period.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence. The attribute requires records showing affected parties were actually notified, and an unsubstantiated claim about standard practice does not establish that notification occurred for the sampled incident.

evidence_summary: The incident record links to a pull request that fixed the vulnerability, merged two days after the incident, but the incident record itself contains no remediation narrative.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: a linked and dated remediation artifact is valid proof even when it lives outside the incident document itself. The linked, merged pull request corroborates that the identified vulnerability was fixed.

evidence_summary: The incident channel's chat log has timestamped messages tracking detection, escalation, mitigation, and resolution, but no separate postmortem document with a formal timeline table was produced.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: a timestamped chat log is a live system record of the response timeline and satisfies the attribute even without a separately authored postmortem document. The timeline, actions, and outcomes are all present in the log.

evidence_summary: When asked about the one personal-data incident in the period, the team said legal handled notifying affected users and regulators, but no notification letter, email, or filing record was provided.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence, especially for a legally consequential notification. Without a record showing data subjects or regulators were actually notified, the attribute cannot be marked as passing.

evidence_summary: The company has no standalone hardening guide, but its Terraform modules and a repository README specify required settings (network rules, instance sizing, logging) for each system type it runs.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: infrastructure-as-code is itself a configuration baseline, often stronger evidence than a prose document since it is enforced, not just described. The IaC templates specify required settings per system type and satisfy the attribute.

evidence_summary: A GitHub branch protection screenshot shows required reviews and status checks on the company's single production repository, which is the entity's only shippable product.
reasoning: Do not import a multi-repo expectation the entity's actual footprint does not have. Coverage of the one repository that constitutes production is complete coverage for a single-product company, so the attribute passes.

evidence_summary: A client-authored spreadsheet lists 'All production changes reviewed and tracked in GitHub' as a claim, with no exported commit history, branch protection screenshot, or other system capture attached.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof. The attribute requires the system configuration itself to show tracking and traceability, and an unverified written assertion about the system is not a substitute for a capture of it.

evidence_summary: The most recent pull request description just says 'fix bug,' but it links to a project-tracker ticket created two days earlier with a fuller change description, opened before any code was written.
reasoning: Verify the whole evidence corpus before failing, not just the first artifact examined. The linked ticket is the pre-implementation documentation the attribute requires, and its creation timestamp precedes the implementation.

evidence_summary: A two-person startup's most recent deploy was self-approved because the co-founder was traveling, but branch protection required a passing CI suite and the author completed a documented self-review checklist before merging.
reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage when the basis is real and documented, and the pass criteria explicitly flag small teams for this treatment rather than an automatic fail. Enforced CI plus a documented self-review checklist is a proportional substitute for a second-person reviewer here.

evidence_summary: The GitHub Actions run log shows the test suite executing and passing on every push, timestamped before the deployment step in the same pipeline, with no separately authored test report document.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a CI pipeline's own pass status is test evidence, not merely a proxy for it, and does not require a separate manually written report. The run log timestamp precedes deployment, satisfying the attribute.

evidence_summary: A solo developer merges and deploys their own pull requests with no second approver, no required CI checks, and no post-deploy review process of any kind documented anywhere.
reasoning: A compensating-control pass must rest on a real, documented basis, not be assumed or silently waived just because the team is small. With no enforced checks and no post-deploy review evidence, there is no compensating control to point to, so unreviewed self-approval is a gap.

evidence_summary: There is no standalone emergency-change document, but the general change management policy has a clearly labeled paragraph defining what qualifies as an emergency, who can authorize expedited deployment, and what retroactive steps are required.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute requires the criteria to exist in writing, not to live in a dedicated standalone document. The embedded paragraph defines emergency criteria, authorization, and retroactive steps, which satisfies the attribute.

evidence_summary: For the single emergency change in the period, the client submitted a spreadsheet row they typed themselves reading 'Hotfix 2026-03-14, prod deploy 02:10, retroactively approved by the CTO 2026-03-15'. The ticketing system and the repository both show the hotfix commit but hold no approval record, and no message or signed acknowledgment from the CTO was provided.
reasoning: A client-typed record that an approval happened is not the approval itself, and the artifact has to come from wherever approvals are actually captured. The line carries an approver name and a date and so looks responsive on its face, but nothing independent of the client's own typing shows the named approver ever reviewed the change.

evidence_summary: A live AWS Organizations console screenshot shows two separate accounts (dev-account, prod-account) with distinct account IDs and separate VPCs, submitted as a generic 'infrastructure screenshot' without a cover note calling out the separation.
reasoning: Live system screenshots are judged on what they show, not on how they were labeled at submission. The console capture plainly shows two distinct accounts, which is sufficient even though nobody wrote 'this proves environment separation' on it.

evidence_summary: A founder-typed architecture diagram (drawn in a slide deck) labels boxes 'Dev' and 'Prod' with no corresponding cloud console export or infrastructure-as-code file to back it up.
reasoning: A client-authored diagram is not system proof of environment separation. Without a console screenshot, IaC file, or account export corroborating the claim, the drawing is just an assertion.

evidence_summary: The company's data handling policy states in writing that production data is never copied to staging or dev, and that synthetic seed data is used instead; no separate masking tool config was submitted.
reasoning: This attribute's pass criteria explicitly accepts a policy confirming production data is absent from non-production, so a documented policy is a valid pass path without a masking tool. The written policy satisfies the requirement and no contrary evidence was submitted.

evidence_summary: An engineer states in a review call that 'we never put real customer data in staging,' but no policy document, masking config, or environment comparison was submitted.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config or policy evidence. Without a written policy or technical control on file, there is nothing to test against for this or future periods.

evidence_summary: An IAM console export lists 2 users with production role bindings versus 6 users with staging/dev role bindings, captured as a raw JSON export rather than a formatted side-by-side comparison table.
reasoning: A live capture plainly showing the substance passes even if it isn't formatted as an explicit before/after comparison. The raw export already demonstrates fewer production users than non-production users.

evidence_summary: A founder-typed spreadsheet lists 'Prod access: 2 people, Staging access: 5 people' with no corresponding IAM console export or role-binding screenshot behind it.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof of access configuration. The claimed numbers need a real IAM export or screenshot corroborating them before they can support a config-attribute pass.

evidence_summary: A GitHub repository settings export shows Dependabot alerts and version updates both enabled, submitted as a plain 'repo settings' screenshot without an explanatory caption.
reasoning: Live system screenshots are judged on what they show regardless of how they were labeled at submission. The export clearly shows dependency tracking and vulnerability alerting configured, which is the substance the attribute requires.

evidence_summary: The security policy document states 'we monitor our dependencies for vulnerabilities,' but no Dependabot, Snyk, or equivalent tool configuration screenshot was submitted.
reasoning: A policy statement is not system proof that a dependency monitoring tool is actually configured and active. Config attributes need a real tool configuration export, not a written intention.

evidence_summary: A CI workflow YAML file in the repository shows a CodeQL static analysis step running on every pull request, submitted as the workflow definition itself rather than a separate scan-results dashboard screenshot.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a live workflow definition that plainly configures and runs a SAST tool on every pull request passes even without a separate results export, since the configuration itself is the evidence the attribute asks for and inherently produces results.

evidence_summary: A vendor's public product page describes 'enterprise-grade static analysis included' for the SaaS platform the company builds on, submitted in place of the company's own CI pipeline configuration.
reasoning: A provider's marketing page is not this organization's own configuration. The company must show its own CI/CD pipeline running static or dynamic analysis on its own application code, not a third party's product description.

evidence_summary: The architecture review checklist embedded in the engineering wiki covers 'who can access this,' 'how is data protected,' and 'what network paths are exposed,' but never uses the literal phrase 'security review.'
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline means judging against the actual required content, not the exact wording. The checklist substantively covers access controls, data protection, and network security, which is what the pass criteria requires.

evidence_summary: No architecture changes occurred during the review period; the engineering team confirms this and no review records exist because there was nothing to review.
reasoning: Default-pass conditions are legitimate: the attribute's own na_condition passes by default when no architecture changes occurred in the period, and that basis should be stated explicitly rather than treated as missing evidence.

evidence_summary: The most recent architecture change moved the bid document store to a new object storage account. A thorough security review record covering access controls, encryption, and network exposure was provided, dated 2026-04-23. The deployment record for the same change shows it went live on 2026-04-14.
reasoning: A security review that follows deployment does not satisfy a criterion that requires the review to precede it. The quality of the review is not what is being tested here, its position in the sequence is, and a review dated nine days after go-live cannot have informed the decision to deploy.

evidence_summary: The BCP/DR content exists as a dedicated section within the company's combined Security and Operations Policy document rather than as its own standalone file, but covers critical systems and recovery procedures in full.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline means judging the required content, not the file structure it lives in. A complete BCP/DR section inside a broader policy document satisfies the attribute just as a standalone file would.

evidence_summary: For a five-person SaaS company, the plan lists RTO/RPO only for the production database and the main application server, the two systems that actually matter, rather than breaking out every individual microservice.
reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: judge against the minimum acceptable design for the company's actual size and architecture. Naming RTO/RPO for the systems that are genuinely critical is sufficient; demanding a granular per-microservice breakdown imports enterprise-scale expectations onto a small team.

evidence_summary: The DR plan's recovery table lists eight systems with the RTO and RPO columns filled in for six of them. For the order management database and the payment reconciliation service the RPO cells read 'TBD'. Both systems are named as critical in the plan's own criticality section.
reasoning: Every system the entity itself calls critical needs both values, so an unfilled cell for one of them fails the attribute no matter how complete the rest of the table looks. TBD is an acknowledgment that the objective has not been set, not an objective.

evidence_summary: Recovery procedures assign responsibility to the role 'Engineering Lead' rather than naming a specific individual by name, since the company is small and roles map one-to-one to people.
reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality applies here too: a role-based assignment is an acceptable form of 'responsible personnel' for a small company, since the mapping from role to person is unambiguous. Demanding an individual's name is a proportionality miss, not a real gap.

evidence_summary: Architecture documentation runs single-region on a single database instance, but includes a written note that multi-region redundancy was evaluated and consciously deferred given current scale, revisiting the decision as the company grows.
reasoning: Never import the neighbor attribute's requirement: this attribute only asks whether resilience was considered in architecture decisions, not whether redundancy was implemented. A documented trade-off decision satisfies the 'considered' bar even when the outcome was to stay single-region.

evidence_summary: The most recent DR test produced no findings requiring changes, and the test report includes a line stating 'no gaps identified, plan remains current' with no corresponding version bump in the plan.
reasoning: Default-pass conditions are legitimate: the attribute explicitly passes when a documented acknowledgment confirms no updates were needed after the test. Absence of a version-history change is expected in that scenario, not a gap.

evidence_summary: A two-person startup ran a manual tabletop walkthrough of its failover steps rather than a live technical DR drill, documented with date, scope, participants, and outcome.
reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage: a documented tabletop walkthrough can stand in for a full technical drill for a very small team, as long as it is real, dated, and shows scope and outcome. The basis for accepting it should be stated explicitly.

evidence_summary: The DR runbook's degraded operations section states that during failover, access stays behind SSO, database encryption is unchanged, and audit logging continues in the standby region.
reasoning: A degraded operations section stating how access control, logging, and data protection continue is exactly the emergency mode content this attribute asks for. A separately titled emergency mode operation plan is not required.

evidence_summary: The BCP commits to restoring service within four hours from backups and walks through the restore procedure, but says nothing about how protections operate while the system runs degraded.
reasoning: Restoration speed is a different question from protection during degraded operations. A plan that only restores service leaves the emergency window unaddressed, which is the specific exposure this attribute tests.

evidence_summary: An RDS console screenshot shows automated backups enabled with a 7-day retention window for the production database, submitted as a plain 'AWS console' capture with no explanatory label.
reasoning: Live system screenshots are judged on what they show, not on how they were labeled at submission. The capture plainly shows automated backups configured, which is what the attribute requires.

evidence_summary: The infrastructure documentation states 'we back up our database automatically every day,' but no AWS console screenshot or backup configuration export was submitted to support the claim.
reasoning: A client-authored description of a backup arrangement is not system proof. Config attributes require an actual provider console export or configuration screenshot, not a written assertion.

evidence_summary: The database has point-in-time recovery enabled with 5-minute granularity, which exceeds the entity's stated 24-hour RPO, but the evidence was submitted as a generic PITR settings screenshot rather than one explicitly labeled 'meets RPO.'
reasoning: No over-literalism: a continuous point-in-time recovery configuration inherently exceeds any daily RPO requirement, and the screenshot showing that granularity is sufficient proof without a separate cover note connecting it to the RPO.

evidence_summary: The internal runbook states backups run 'nightly,' but the AWS Backup plan console export actually shows the schedule configured to run weekly.
reasoning: A config attribute is judged against the real system state, not the written description of it. The corroborating export contradicts the documented schedule, so the actual weekly frequency is what gets tested against the RPO.

evidence_summary: A CloudWatch alarm configuration export shows an SNS topic wired to a Slack channel that fires on backup job failure, submitted as a plain alarm-rules screenshot rather than one showing a live test failure notification.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a live capture of an alarm configured to alert on backup failure passes even without a demonstrated real failure event, since the attribute tests that alerting is configured, not that a failure has occurred.

evidence_summary: The operations policy states 'the team monitors backup jobs and would notice if one failed,' with no CloudWatch alarm, SNS topic, or equivalent alerting configuration submitted.
reasoning: Verbal or policy-level assurance is never config evidence. The attribute requires an actual alerting configuration export showing automated notification on failure, not a description of team vigilance.

evidence_summary: A Terraform configuration file in the infrastructure repository defines S3 cross-region replication from the primary bucket to a bucket in a different AWS region, submitted as the IaC source rather than a console screenshot.
reasoning: Live evidence is judged on what it shows regardless of format: an infrastructure-as-code file that plainly configures cross-region replication is system evidence just as a console screenshot would be, and it passes on that basis.

evidence_summary: The architecture documentation asserts 'our backups are stored in a separate region for durability,' but no AWS console export, replication configuration, or storage bucket listing was submitted to verify it.
reasoning: A written architecture claim is not system proof of the actual storage configuration. The geographic separation of backups is a config attribute that needs an actual export showing the regions involved.

evidence_summary: For a small SaaS company, the compute layer runs in an auto-scaling group configured to automatically relaunch instances in a different availability zone if the primary zone becomes unavailable, rather than a full active-active multi-region deployment.
reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: judge against the minimum acceptable design for the company's actual scale, and the pass criteria itself accepts a multi-AZ deployment. An automated cross-AZ relaunch capability is a legitimate failover mechanism; demanding full multi-region active-active infrastructure imports enterprise-scale expectations.

evidence_summary: A founder-drawn architecture diagram shows arrows labeled 'failover' pointing to a secondary region, but the actual cloud console shows only a single-AZ, single-region deployment with no standby instances configured.
reasoning: A drawn diagram is not system proof of an actual failover capability. Config attributes require the real cloud configuration to show alternate processing infrastructure, and here the console contradicts the diagram.

evidence_summary: The founder restored a recent database backup into a scratch environment as part of routine practice, documenting the date, the backup restored, and the successful outcome, rather than running a formal enterprise-style DR exercise.
reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage: an informal but real and documented restoration test satisfies the attribute for a small team, as long as date, scope, and outcome are captured. Formality of process is not the bar, evidence of an actual successful restore is.

evidence_summary: The restoration test record is dated five months ago and documents scope and date properly. Its outcome section reads 'restore completed with errors on two tables, rental history incomplete, to be re-tested next cycle.' No later test record was provided.
reasoning: This attribute asks for a successful restoration test, and a documented failure is a documented failure however recent or well recorded it is. An intention to re-test is not a test, so the entity has not demonstrated it can actually recover from its backups.

evidence_summary: The vendor register is a live Airtable base with a populated risk-tier column for every vendor; the evidence submitted is a screenshot of that base rather than a formal exported document.
reasoning: Live system screenshots are system evidence regardless of the label attached at submission. The screenshot plainly shows a maintained inventory with risk tiers populated per vendor, which is what the attribute requires.

evidence_summary: The vendor management policy has an 'Issue Handling' section naming an escalation contact and a remediation deadline, but does not use the exact phrase 'security issue escalation process.'
reasoning: Judge substance over exact phrasing, not the presence of a matching heading. The section describes escalation steps and remediation expectations, which satisfies the attribute even without itemized sub-headings.

evidence_summary: Vendor termination steps live in an offboarding checklist while the data-return clause is in the standard MSA template used for all vendor contracts; no single document contains both.
reasoning: A live capture plainly showing the substance passes even when it is spread across the entity's normal set of documents rather than one file. Together the checklist and MSA clause describe termination plus data return/destruction, satisfying the attribute.

evidence_summary: The vendor procedure names a shared Slack channel and a designated security contact for reporting vendor issues, but has no section formally titled 'Communication Protocol.'
reasoning: No over-literalism: a live document showing the substance passes even if it is not itemized under a matching heading. Naming a channel and contact is a communication protocol in substance.

evidence_summary: A client-maintained vendor tracker spreadsheet has a column marked 'Security clause: Yes' for each vendor, but no actual contract or MSA excerpt was pulled to confirm the clause language.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof of a contract's contents. The attribute requires the actual contract or MSA text showing the security clause, not a self-reported tracker entry.

evidence_summary: A two-person AI-native startup onboarded one critical payment vendor; no formal SOC 2 report was obtained, but the founder documented a short review note citing the vendor's published security attestation page before signing.
reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage, and for a solo/small team a documented review of a vendor's public attestation stands in for an unobtainable formal audit report. The basis is real and documented, so it passes on a proportional basis.

evidence_summary: The last manual reassessment note for a critical vendor is 14 months old, but the entity uses an automated vendor-risk platform that continuously monitors that vendor's SOC 2 report expiry and would flag any lapse.
reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path: continuous automated monitoring of a vendor's certification status can stand in for a periodic manual reassessment when the basis is real and verifiable. The gap should not be called purely on the age of the last manual note.

evidence_summary: The vendor manager states verbally that the confidentiality NDA with a data-access vendor was signed, but no signed document or contract clause was pulled as evidence.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config or record evidence. The attribute requires an actual signed NDA or confidentiality clause on file, not an assertion that one exists.

evidence_summary: A data processing addendum for a vendor handling personal data is a Google Doc still marked 'DRAFT' with an unfilled signature block and no approval date.
reasoning: A draft document is not an adopted or executed agreement. Draft banners and an empty signature block mean the commitment was never actually made, regardless of how complete the content looks.

evidence_summary: The subservice organization list lives on an internal wiki page naming AWS and the payment processor with their control areas; the evidence captured is a screenshot of that live page rather than an exported file.
reasoning: Live system screenshots are valid system evidence regardless of submission label. The page plainly identifies the dependent vendors and their control areas, satisfying the attribute.

evidence_summary: The cloud provider's public trust page states 'SOC 2 Type II certified,' and that page was accepted as the vendor's report without the actual PDF report being obtained or on file.
reasoning: A provider's marketing or trust page is not this org's actual audit report. The attribute requires the report itself on file, not a public certification claim.

evidence_summary: A dependent vendor's SOC 2 report period ended three months before the entity's examination period began, but a signed bridge letter from the vendor covers the intervening gap through the examination end date.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: the pass criteria explicitly allow a bridge letter to cover a gap between report period and examination period, so this clause must not be skipped when it is present. The bridge letter satisfies coverage of the examination period.

evidence_summary: SOC 2 reports are on file for both dependent vendors. The cloud provider's report period runs through two months before the examination date. The payment processor's report period ended eight months before it, and no bridge letter covering the interval was requested or provided.
reasoning: Holding a vendor's report is not the same as being covered for the period under examination, which is what this attribute tests. An eight month uncovered interval needs a bridge letter, and its absence leaves the entity relying on controls nobody has reported on for most of the period.

evidence_summary: The review of each vendor's SOC 2 report is recorded as a row in a shared tracker spreadsheet (vendor, reviewer, date, exceptions noted), with complementary user-entity controls listed in a separate onboarding doc rather than a single narrative memo.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and use of the review process, not on the format or consolidation of its documentation. A tracker row plus a separate CSOC list together show the report was reviewed and vendor-operated controls documented.

evidence_summary: A live screenshot of the company's cloud security dashboard, showing dated automated compliance-check results over the past quarter, was tagged generically as 'document' at intake rather than as a system capture.
reasoning: Live system screenshots are system evidence regardless of how they were labeled at submission. Judge what the capture actually shows, dated, regularly produced monitoring output, not the intake tag it was filed under.

evidence_summary: A weekly 'monitoring log' spreadsheet is manually typed by an employee, listing entries like 'checked dashboard, all good' with no attached screenshots, exports, or system-generated timestamps.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof. Monitoring evidence needs an actual system output (dashboard capture, alert log, automated report) behind the claim, not a self-reported log describing that a check happened.

evidence_summary: Management's quarterly security posture review happened on a recorded video call; the only record is a dated Slack thread summarizing the discussion with the two attendees named and key decisions listed.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a dated Slack summary naming attendees and covering the substance of a security posture review satisfies this attribute even though it isn't a formal report document. Judge the content, not the medium.

evidence_summary: A 5-person startup has no internal audit function; instead, an independent third-party penetration testing firm performed a full assessment 8 months ago and delivered a dated report to leadership.
reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage: for a company this size, an independent external assessment stands in for a nonexistent internal audit function. Pass explicitly on this compensating basis.

evidence_summary: Submitted as the independent evaluation: a thorough self assessment against the control list, dated four months ago, performed and signed by the engineering lead. That same person owns access provisioning, change management, and the monitoring configuration the assessment covers.
reasoning: Independence in this attribute is about who performed the evaluation, not how rigorous it was, and a person cannot provide it over controls they operate. A careful self assessment is real evidence for management review, and that is a different attribute from this one.

evidence_summary: The company's incident response policy has a subsection defining deficiency severity levels (critical/high/medium/low) and triage criteria, but there is no standalone 'Deficiency Management Policy' document.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute asks whether a documented process for identifying and rating deficiency severity exists, not that it live in a separately titled policy. Content embedded in a related policy satisfies the requirement.

evidence_summary: The engagement's internal risk policy has a clause stating identified control deficiencies must be reported to the CEO within 24 hours and to the board at the next scheduled meeting, but the clause sits inside a general 'Governance' section rather than a document titled for deficiency communication.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a clear, documented escalation path with defined timing and named recipients satisfies this attribute regardless of which document section it appears in.

evidence_summary: The corrective action tracker template has 'Owner' and 'Due Date' columns, but the one populated example row shows Owner as 'TBD' and Due Date blank.
reasoning: Structural existence of the right columns is not enough; the pass criteria require an actual example with both fields populated. An unassigned owner and missing timeline in the only real entry means the requirement is not met in practice.

evidence_summary: A 3-person company's only deficiency during the period (a misconfigured storage bucket permission) was fixed the same day; the only record is a Slack thread with a before screenshot, the fix, and an after screenshot confirming closure, timestamped throughout.
reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: a small company's real, timestamped Slack thread showing the deficiency identified and tracked through to a confirmed fix is a proportional substitute for a formal ticketing tool. Pass explicitly on this proportional basis.

evidence_summary: The entity runs on managed Supabase Postgres and Vercel with no custom CloudWatch-style alarms configured, but the Supabase project dashboard natively displays CPU, connection, and storage utilization by default.
reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path: a managed platform's built-in capacity dashboard satisfies 'capacity metrics are monitored' even without the entity configuring its own alarms, since the metrics are actually being collected and visible.

evidence_summary: A generic architecture diagram labeled 'monitoring in place' was submitted as evidence that CPU and storage utilization are tracked, with no actual dashboard, export, or config shown.
reasoning: A diagram asserting a practice is not system proof of it. The attribute requires an actual monitoring platform view or export showing metrics being collected, not a claim illustrated in a diagram.

evidence_summary: Capacity alerts are configured to post to a shared on-call Slack channel monitored on a rotation, rather than paging one named individual.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: the pass criteria accept any defined notification target including chat, and do not require a specific named recipient. A monitored shared channel satisfies the notification requirement.

evidence_summary: CloudWatch alarms for capacity thresholds exist and were credited as configured, but the alarm state shown is 'INSUFFICIENT_DATA' because the alarms are not actually receiving live metric data.
reasoning: An alarm that exists on paper but is not receiving live data is not functioning alerting. The evidence must show the alarm is actively evaluating real metrics, not merely defined.

evidence_summary: A documented manual capacity expansion procedure defines clear trigger thresholds and expansion steps, but the entity has never had to invoke it since no capacity threshold has been approached.
reasoning: The pass criteria explicitly treat a documented but never-exercised manual procedure as a flagged pass for CPA review, not an outright fail. A defined procedure with real trigger criteria satisfies the design-stage requirement even absent invocation.

evidence_summary: Auto-scaling is enabled only on the web application tier; the production database, which also serves customer traffic, has no scaling or expansion configuration and no documented expansion procedure at all.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline requires coverage of production systems generally, not just the tier that happens to have scaling enabled. Partial coverage that excludes a production data store with neither auto-scaling nor a documented procedure is a systematic gap, not a pass.

evidence_summary: Eight months ago the founder posted a Slack message comparing current usage against projected growth and concluding current capacity was adequate; no formal capacity planning report was produced.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the substance of the review being performed, not the formality of its write-up. The Slack message documents an actual comparison of current versus forecasted demand within the required window.

evidence_summary: A live product spec doc in the company's engineering wiki describes exactly what each API endpoint processes, expected latency targets, and uptime commitments, but never uses the literal phrase 'functional requirements' or 'nonfunctional requirements'.
reasoning: Judge what the evidence shows, not whether it uses the exact vocabulary of the attribute text. The spec document substantively covers what the system processes (functional) and performance/availability targets (nonfunctional), which is all the criteria requires.

evidence_summary: A 40-page product requirements document describes dispatch matching, courier assignment, and order state transitions in detail. It contains no performance targets, no accuracy expectations for the matching logic, and no availability commitment. The client noted those live 'in the SLA we give enterprise customers', but no such document was provided.
reasoning: This attribute names two categories of requirement and both have to be documented, so a strong functional specification with nothing nonfunctional in it is half the evidence. A reference to targets living in an unproduced customer contract does not document them for the entity's own processing.

evidence_summary: An API schema document lists every input field with its data type and format, and a separate integration guide identifies which upstream system or user action produces each field, but the two facts live in different sections rather than one unified table.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the criteria only requires that inputs, sources, and formats be defined somewhere in the entity's documentation, not consolidated into a single artifact. Between the schema doc and the integration guide, both required facts are present and traceable.

evidence_summary: The company made no significant processing changes during the review period, and there is no formal review record or version history entry to point to.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes with an explicit pass-by-default clause pass when the triggering event never occurred, not on the presence of a review record. The pass criteria for this attribute states that no significant changes occurring during the period is a pass by default, so the absence of a review log is not itself a gap.

evidence_summary: Input characteristics are enforced through a TypeScript/Zod schema in the codebase (field types, string length ranges, enum values) rather than a written data dictionary, and a screenshot of the schema file was submitted as evidence.
reasoning: Live system evidence counts regardless of the format it was submitted in. A code-level schema defining types, formats, and ranges is a legitimate documented definition of expected input characteristics even though it is not a prose document.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of API middleware code shows a validation decorator running on every incoming request that returns a 422 error with field-level messages when a payload fails schema checks.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: a code screenshot showing active validation logic at the entry point is system configuration evidence, not merely a description of one. The rejection behavior shown satisfies the criteria even though it was not captured from an admin panel toggle.

evidence_summary: The client submitted a spreadsheet they typed themselves listing 'Input validation: Yes, all fields checked' with no accompanying code, config screenshot, or system export.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof; a config-state claim needs a capture of the actual system behavior or a corroborating export. A self-typed assertion of 'yes we validate' carries no evidentiary weight on its own for a config attribute.

evidence_summary: A logging platform screenshot shows request records with timestamp and originating IP/user-agent columns, but the column is labeled 'client' rather than the phrase 'source identifier'.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a column that identifies the request's originating client or user is a source identifier in substance, regardless of its header label. The screenshot plainly shows the required timestamped, source-identified records even though each is not itemized by the attribute's exact wording.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the request-logging configuration clearly shows input records are automatically purged after 30 days, and the AI passed it because the records themselves carry timestamps and source identifiers.
reasoning: A records-retention config attribute fails when the captured setting falls below its explicit floor, however complete the records themselves are. Input records purged at 30 days do not meet the 90-day minimum, so well-formed timestamps and source identifiers do not rescue a retention window below the required threshold.

evidence_summary: An internal engineering RFC in Notion walks through how a billing calculation job takes raw usage events and produces an invoice, defining what counts as a correct output, but the document is titled 'Billing Pipeline Design' rather than 'Processing Specification'.
reasoning: Judge what the evidence shows, not its title or label. The RFC describes expected processing behavior for a key activity including inputs, outputs, and correctness definition, which is exactly what this attribute requires.

evidence_summary: The processing specification walks each pipeline stage from meter file ingestion to billing export, naming the inputs and the outputs of every stage. Nothing in it defines what a complete or accurate run means: no reconciliation rule between records received and records posted, no tolerance, and no definition of a successfully processed reading.
reasoning: This attribute asks for expected behavior and for how completeness and accuracy are defined, so an input to output map without either definition is only part of the specification. Without a stated definition there is no standard against which a run can be judged wrong, which is what makes processing integrity testable at all.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the monitoring platform shows an active alert rule that fires when a processing job's failure rate exceeds a threshold, routed to an on-call channel, for the company's core billing pipeline.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: this is a config attribute, so the config screenshot itself is the correct and sufficient evidence type; it should not be held to a document attribute's expectation of a separate written error-handling policy. The active alert rule is the error detection mechanism the criteria asks for.

evidence_summary: The client submitted a spreadsheet they manually typed titled 'Known Processing Errors Log' with a handful of rows, but no screenshot or export from an actual monitoring or exception-handling system was provided.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a config-state claim; it needs provenance from the monitoring system itself. A typed list of 'errors we noticed' does not establish that an automated detection mechanism is actually active.

evidence_summary: Every processing job writes a transaction record with a timestamp to the cloud platform's native audit-log service, retained for one year, but there is no separate application-managed 'processing log' table in the company's own database.
reasoning: Judge whether timestamped activity records are retained for the required period, not whether they live in a purpose-built table. Transaction records captured in the platform's native audit-log service with timestamps and one-year retention satisfy the traceability requirement regardless of where they physically reside.

evidence_summary: An engineer said in a walkthrough call that processing records are kept 'well past 90 days' but did not share any screenshot, export, or configuration page from the logging system.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config evidence. A retention duration claim for a config attribute requires an actual capture of the system's retention setting or a records export demonstrating the timespan.

evidence_summary: No processing errors occurred at the company during the review period, and there is no error-correction record to sample because there was nothing to correct.
reasoning: Process-exists sample attributes pass on the existence and use of the correction process, and this one explicitly passes by default when no errors occurred during the period. Marking a gap for having no sample to draw from ignores the pass criteria's own default-pass clause.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the cloud storage bucket's IAM policy shows read/write access scoped only to the application's service role, with all public and cross-account access explicitly denied.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: this is a config attribute, so the IAM policy screenshot itself is the correct evidence, not a substitute awaiting a separate written access-control policy document. The configuration plainly restricts output access to authorized identities, satisfying the criteria.

evidence_summary: The client submitted a one-page internal memo stating 'all outputs are access-controlled' with no accompanying IAM, database grant, or API permission screenshot.
reasoning: A client-authored document is not system proof for a config-state claim; the actual access-control configuration must be captured. An assertion memo with no underlying export or screenshot cannot establish that unauthorized access is actually blocked.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the API gateway's authorization middleware code shows every output-serving endpoint requiring a valid signed token tied to a specific recipient account before returning data.
reasoning: No over-literalism: code-level authorization enforcement is a legitimate control restricting output distribution to intended recipients, even though it is not a firewall rule or delivery-service setting. The evidence plainly shows the substance the criteria requires.

evidence_summary: The evidence submitted for this attribute is a screenshot of the company's cloud hosting provider's public marketing page describing 'enterprise-grade access controls' as a platform feature.
reasoning: A provider's marketing or trust page is not this organization's own configuration. The criteria requires evidence of how this entity restricts its own output distribution, not a vendor's general capability claims.

evidence_summary: A screenshot shows an automated job that reconciles the record count of a generated export file against the source query before the file is written to the delivery bucket, but the pipeline step is not labeled 'pre-delivery verification'.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a live capture plainly showing the reconciliation step occurring before delivery satisfies the criteria even though the step is not itemized with that exact label. The pipeline order itself demonstrates the check happens prior to output distribution.

evidence_summary: The client submitted a spreadsheet they typed listing 'output checked manually before sending' for a handful of dates, with no export, log, or screenshot of an actual verification check.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof; a verification-mechanism claim needs an actual system export or screenshot showing the check ran. A self-typed log of asserted manual reviews does not establish that a real verification mechanism exists.

evidence_summary: Every output delivery is recorded with a timestamp in the company's transactional email/webhook provider dashboard, retained for six months, rather than in the company's own database.
reasoning: Records the entity maintains in its delivery provider's system are still the entity's own output-activity records when they show timestamps and adequate retention. Six months of timestamped delivery events meets the 90-day floor, and their location in the provider's dashboard rather than an in-house table is not a deficiency.

evidence_summary: The client submitted a spreadsheet they typed listing output deliveries by date, presented as the delivery log, with no export or screenshot from the actual delivery-logging system.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof; an output-activity-record claim needs a capture of the system that actually records deliveries. A hand-typed list of dates does not establish that timestamped delivery records are genuinely maintained by the system.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the production database's role grants shows only the application's service account has UPDATE/DELETE privileges on core tables, with all other roles restricted to read-only or no access.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: this is a config attribute, so the role-grant screenshot itself is the correct evidence, not a placeholder awaiting a separate written data-protection policy. The configuration directly demonstrates that unauthorized modification or deletion is blocked.

evidence_summary: The client submitted an internal spreadsheet they typed themselves titled 'DB Permissions' summarizing who supposedly has write access, with no screenshot or export from the database or storage system itself.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof; a config-state claim about database permissions requires a capture of the actual role grants or an export corroborated by a system view. A hand-typed summary does not establish the real configuration.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the database schema shows foreign-key constraints and NOT NULL checks enforcing referential integrity, plus a nightly checksum-comparison script log confirming no drift, but neither artifact is labeled 'data integrity check'.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a live capture plainly showing referential integrity constraints and checksum verification passes even though the underlying mechanisms are not itemized under the attribute's exact wording. The substance of an integrity mechanism is present.

evidence_summary: The evidence submitted is a screenshot of the cloud storage provider's public durability claim ('99.999999999% durability') from their marketing page, offered as proof of this org's stored-data integrity.
reasoning: A provider's marketing or trust page is not this organization's own configuration. The criteria requires evidence of integrity mechanisms this entity has in place, not a vendor's generic durability marketing statistic.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the cloud archive bucket shows object-lock retention configured to match the entity's stated retention requirement, with delete and overwrite operations blocked for the locked period, but there is no separate written archival policy document.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: this is a config attribute, so the enforced retention-lock configuration itself is the correct and sufficient evidence, not a stand-in awaiting a written policy. The screenshot demonstrates both the retention period and its protection from modification.

evidence_summary: The client submitted a spreadsheet they typed describing a retention schedule by data type, with no screenshot or export of the actual archive storage configuration enforcing it.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof; a retention-enforcement claim needs a capture of the actual archive configuration. A described schedule with no corroborating system evidence does not establish that retention is actually enforced.

evidence_summary: The cloud provider's audit trail for the storage bucket retains create/modify/delete events with user identifiers for over 180 days, and the same view shows the retention setting, but the submitted screenshot is filtered to the most recent two weeks of events.
reasoning: No over-literalism: judge the underlying retention configuration shown in the capture, not the narrow date filter applied to the event list. The audit-trail retention setting visible in the same view exceeds the 90-day minimum, so a two-week filtered event list should not be read as the total retained history.

evidence_summary: An engineer said in a Slack message shared as evidence that 'storage changes are tracked' but no audit-log export, screenshot, or configuration reference was provided.
reasoning: Verbal or chat confirmation is never config evidence. A storage-activity-record claim for a config attribute requires an actual export or screenshot of the audit trail, not a message asserting that tracking happens.
