evidence_summary: A screenshot of the account sign-up flow shows a linked privacy notice presented to the user before they submit any personal information, but there is no separately hosted, publicly indexed privacy page.
reasoning: Judge what the evidence shows: a documented delivery channel at the point of collection satisfies the criteria just as well as a standalone public URL. The sign-up flow screenshot demonstrates the notice was accessible before or at the time of collection, which is exactly what is required.

evidence_summary: The published privacy notice has a section titled 'Who We Share Data With' listing categories of vendors and partners receiving data, covering the third-party disclosure requirement without using that phrase verbatim.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the criteria checks for the substantive presence of each required element, not a section titled with the exact regulatory phrase. A section describing who data is shared with satisfies the third-party disclosure requirement.

evidence_summary: The published privacy notice covers the categories of personal information collected, why each is used, the named third parties it is shared with, and how learners exercise access and deletion rights. It never describes which entities or activities it covers; the company operates the tutoring marketplace and a separate assessment product under different brands.
reasoning: All five elements are required and the description of covered entities and activities is the one most often absent, so a notice that reads as thorough can still fail on scope. Where an entity runs more than one product, a notice that never says which entities and activities it governs leaves a data subject unable to tell whether it applies to them.

evidence_summary: The privacy notice was last substantively updated 10 months ago according to the internal version-history log in the CMS, but the public-facing page itself does not display a visible 'last updated' date to a casual reader.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: the underlying version-history record establishes the notice is current within 24 months, which is what the criteria actually tests, even though that date is not surfaced as a footer timestamp on the page itself.

evidence_summary: The privacy notice lives in the company's website content repository, where every prior version is preserved in commit history along with the date each change was published, and change announcements go out via an in-app banner; there is no formal public web-archive tool in use.
reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: judge against a realistic minimum design rather than requiring a dedicated archiving product. A repository's version history preserving every prior notice, paired with a real in-app notification mechanism for changes, is a proportional and verifiable way to meet this requirement.

evidence_summary: The consent screen at sign-up includes one sentence noting that declining the optional data-sharing toggle will disable certain personalization features, rather than a dedicated 'consequences of denying consent' section.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the criteria requires that consequences of denying consent be communicated, not that they occupy a labeled section of their own. A brief but clear statement of what happens if consent is declined satisfies the substance of the requirement.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the cookie-consent banner is paired with a database table screenshot showing consent records stored with timestamp and user identifier for each acceptance, but there is no separate written consent-management policy document.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: this is a config attribute, so the consent-capture mechanism and its stored records are the correct and sufficient evidence, not a placeholder awaiting a written policy. The configuration demonstrates consent is obtained and recorded exactly as the criteria requires.

evidence_summary: The client submitted a spreadsheet they manually typed logging 'consents received' by date and user name, with no export or screenshot from the actual consent-capture system or database.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof; a consent-record claim for a config attribute needs a capture of the system that actually stores consent. A hand-typed log does not establish that consent is genuinely captured and retained by the system.

evidence_summary: The signup flow screenshot shows an unbundled, separately checked consent for the health and dietary information collected about children in care. The vendor register shows the support desk tool processes ticket contents, including that information, in another region; consent for that transfer is covered only by acceptance of the general terms at signup.
reasoning: This attribute has two triggers and separate explicit consent is required for each one that is present, so satisfying it for sensitive information does not satisfy it for cross-border transfer. Bundling the transfer into general terms acceptance is exactly the bundling the criteria exclude.

evidence_summary: The company did not introduce any new uses for previously collected personal information during the review period, and there is no re-consent notification or new-purposes procedure document to point to.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes with an explicit pass-by-default clause pass when the triggering event never occurred. The pass criteria for this attribute states that no new purposes introduced during the period is a pass by default, so the absence of a re-consent process document is not itself a gap.

evidence_summary: A comparison of the production database schema against the privacy notice shows a hashed device identifier field used only for fraud prevention, which the AI flagged as undisclosed collection, though the notice's general 'device and usage information' clause covers it.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a general category disclosure in the privacy notice can cover a specific field without listing every field name individually. The hashed device identifier falls within the disclosed 'device and usage information' category, so this is not undisclosed collection.

evidence_summary: The evidence submitted for this attribute is a screenshot of a third-party analytics vendor's public page describing their own data-minimization practices, offered as proof of what personal information this org collects.
reasoning: A provider's marketing or trust page is not this organization's own configuration. The criteria requires a comparison of this entity's actual collected data fields against its own privacy notice, not a vendor's unrelated public claims.

evidence_summary: A data-flow document in the company wiki lists each category of personal information, its collection method, and its source, with the legal-basis column filled in tersely as 'legitimate interest' or 'consent' for every row rather than a detailed legal analysis.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and identification of the required content, not on the depth or polish of its write-up. A terse but present legal-basis designation for each category satisfies the criteria, which only asks that a legal basis be identified.

evidence_summary: The data map documents eleven collection points captured directly from users, each with its method and a stated legal basis. It is silent on the two data enrichment vendors from which the company buys additional business contact records, which the vendor register and two invoices confirm are in use.
reasoning: A collection inventory has to cover every source personal information arrives from, not only the ones where the data subject is present. Acquired records are the collection method most often left out of a data map and the most likely to lack a legal basis, so omitting that source entirely is a gap rather than an incomplete detail.

evidence_summary: The company did not acquire any additional personal information beyond its original collection scope during the review period, and there is no notification record or procedure document specific to that scenario.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes with an explicit pass-by-default clause pass when the triggering event never occurred. The pass criteria for this attribute states that no additional information acquired during the period is a pass by default, so the absence of a notification record is not itself a gap.

evidence_summary: No personal information was retained beyond its original collection purpose during the review period, so there is no consent-to-retain record to sample.
reasoning: Process-exists sample attributes pass on the existence and use of the consent-to-retain process, and this one explicitly passes by default when no such retention occurred during the period. Requiring a consent record to exist when the underlying trigger never happened ignores the pass criteria's own default-pass clause.

evidence_summary: The company's privacy policy has a 'How We Use Your Information' section listing each disclosed purpose, and the product's admin console restricts analytics/marketing feature access by role so engineers can't repurpose data outside those listed uses.
reasoning: A pass-criteria clause is satisfied by substance, not by matching a specific document title. The pass criteria names 'access restrictions by purpose' as an accepted form, so the policy section plus the role-gated feature access together constitute a real purpose-limitation control even without a document literally titled 'Purpose Limitation Policy.'

evidence_summary: A live screenshot of the analytics platform's data-category settings shows only the categories listed in the privacy notice (product usage, billing) are enabled; no marketing or resale categories are toggled on.
reasoning: Live system screenshots are system evidence regardless of how they were labeled at submission, this was filed generically as 'screenshot' rather than a formal data-processing inventory, but it plainly shows actual uses matching disclosed purposes. Judge what the evidence shows, not its filename.

evidence_summary: The founder typed up a spreadsheet titled 'Our data uses' listing the same purposes as the privacy notice, with no export or screenshot from any actual system pulling this from configuration.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a config attribute, it asserts alignment rather than demonstrating it. Actual-use claims need provenance (a system export/screenshot) or corroboration against a live system view, not a hand-typed restatement of the policy.

evidence_summary: A support-team runbook article walks through how a data access request comes into the shared inbox, how the requester's identity is checked, how the export is generated, and a 30-day SLA badge on the ticket queue, but the article is titled 'Handling Data Requests,' not 'Data Subject Rights Policy.'
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and use of the process, not on matching a specific document title. The runbook covers intake, verification, fulfillment, and timeframe, everything the attribute asks for, so it passes despite the informal name.

evidence_summary: Access requests are only fulfilled after the requester logs into their existing authenticated account session; there is no separate ID-check or email-confirmation step beyond the standard login.
reasoning: Never import a stricter requirement than the attribute text specifies, the pass criteria names account authentication explicitly alongside email confirmation and ID verification. Existing account authentication is a legitimate identity-verification method, so requiring a redundant separate step over-reads the attribute.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the account settings page shows editable name, email, and preference fields the user can change directly and save, filed under a generic 'UI screenshots' evidence batch rather than a dedicated privacy-rights folder.
reasoning: A live capture plainly showing self-service update capability passes even when it wasn't itemized or filed under a privacy-specific label. The screenshot demonstrates the exact mechanism the attribute asks for.

evidence_summary: The company's public marketing site states 'You can update your information anytime in your dashboard,' but no screenshot or export of the actual settings page was provided.
reasoning: A provider's marketing or public-facing page is not proof of the product's actual configuration. The attribute requires evidence the self-service mechanism exists in the live system, not a promise made on a marketing page.

evidence_summary: A two-person startup has never received or denied a data access or correction request, and has no denial-letter template on file.
reasoning: Apply the criteria's own default-pass clause before flagging an absence as a gap, the pass criteria explicitly states this attribute passes by default when no denials have occurred. A naive read fails it for lacking an artifact the criteria says isn't required in this scenario.

evidence_summary: The client stated no access or correction requests were denied, so no denial letters were provided. The request log they supplied shows two requests closed with the status 'rejected, could not verify', and the outbound messages for both read in full 'We are unable to process this request at this time.'
reasoning: A pass by default for a non-occurrence fails the moment the entity's own log shows the event occurred, whatever the client believes happened. Two requests were denied, and the messages sent carry neither a written reason nor any appeal instruction, which is precisely what this attribute requires a denial to include.

evidence_summary: The data-subject-rights runbook defines a 30-day response window and a named owner, and the company has never received an access or correction request in its operating history, so there are no fulfilled tickets to sample.
reasoning: At the design/Type I stage this attribute passes when a defined response timeframe is in place and no requests have been received, the criteria states this default explicitly. There is no sample to draw because the triggering event never occurred, so treating the empty sample as a gap misapplies the criteria.

evidence_summary: Vendor data-processing agreements contain confidentiality and purpose-limitation clauses restricting each subprocessor to the specific services they were engaged for, but there is no standalone 'third-party disclosure policy' document.
reasoning: Never import a stricter requirement than the attribute text specifies, the pass criteria asks for controls restricting disclosure to approved purposes and privacy requirements communicated to third parties, and contractual purpose-limitation clauses satisfy exactly that. A standalone policy document is one way to satisfy it, not the only way.

evidence_summary: The privacy policy restricts disclosure to approved purposes, and signed data processing agreements are on file for the three largest processors. Two further vendors that receive couple and guest contact details, an email delivery service and a post-event survey tool, have no privacy terms on file; both were onboarded directly by the marketing lead.
reasoning: The requirement to communicate privacy requirements before disclosure applies to every third party that receives personal information, not to the ones large enough to have gone through procurement. Agreements covering the major processors leave the smaller recipients unbound, and those are usually the ones acquired outside any review.

evidence_summary: An export from the company's integration platform lists each outbound data-sharing event with destination, data fields, and timestamp, submitted as a raw CSV export rather than a formatted 'disclosure register.'
reasoning: A system export is system evidence regardless of its formatting or filename, it shows recipient, data type, date, and purpose exactly as required. Don't fail evidence for lacking a polished presentation when the substance is a genuine system-generated record.

evidence_summary: A spreadsheet titled 'Vendor disclosures 2026' was typed up by the ops lead from memory, listing vendor names and rough dates, with no underlying system log or export to corroborate the entries.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet reconstructed from memory is not reliable disclosure proof, records need to be system-maintained or corroborated against an actual system view, with the recipient/data/date/purpose fields the criteria requires. Recall-based entries missing timestamps and a source system carry no evidentiary weight.

evidence_summary: The company's incident-tracking tool has a 'Privacy Breach' category that has never had an entry logged against it; the tracker itself was set up eight months ago and shows zero incidents.
reasoning: Config attributes for a register pass on the mechanism existing, not on it having contents, the pass criteria explicitly treats an empty register as a pass when no breaches occurred. Flagging an empty-but-functional register as a gap misapplies the criteria's own default.

evidence_summary: In an interview, the head of engineering said 'we'd log any breach in our internal tracker if one happened,' but no screenshot, export, or actual tracker view was provided.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config evidence, a described capability with no system capture to back it up doesn't demonstrate the mechanism actually exists. The attribute needs a record or screenshot of the tracker itself, not an assurance about it.

evidence_summary: The standard vendor MSA includes a clause requiring immediate remediation, corrective action, and a right to terminate on discovery of unauthorized data use, but there is no separate 'third-party misuse remediation procedure' document.
reasoning: Never fail an attribute for lacking a specific artifact form when the criteria's own substance is met by another form, the criteria asks for remediation steps (investigation, contract enforcement, relationship termination), and the MSA clause describes exactly those. A standalone procedure document is not required.

evidence_summary: A solo-founder company has two subprocessors (a cloud host and an email provider); the founder documented, in a short vendor-review note, that both publish current SOC 2 reports and that their standard DPAs include breach-notification clauses, but no formal privacy-assessment questionnaire was completed.
reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage, for a solo founder, a documented review of a vendor's public security attestation plus the DPA's breach clause stands in for a formal assessment questionnaire. The basis is real, verifiable, and documented, so it passes on a proportional basis.

evidence_summary: An internal breach-response runbook contains a table mapping each jurisdiction to its notification deadline (72 hours to the EU supervisory authority, affected individuals without undue delay, applicable US state AG notifications) and the contractual customer-notice terms, but it lives as an appendix to the incident response plan rather than a document titled 'Breach Reporting Requirements.'
reasoning: Identification of breach-reporting requirements passes on substance regardless of the document's title or location. The runbook table actually names the regulatory timelines, recipients, and contractual obligations the criteria asks for, so failing it for not being a standalone titled document imports a form requirement the attribute doesn't state.

evidence_summary: The breach notification timeline, responsible-party assignment, and required notification content are all defined within a section of the company's broader incident response plan rather than in a standalone breach-notification document.
reasoning: Never import a requirement the attribute text doesn't state, nothing in the criteria requires a standalone document, only that timelines, responsible parties, and content are defined somewhere. A well-integrated section of the incident response plan satisfies the same substance.

evidence_summary: The incident response plan's breach section reads in full: 'In the event of a breach of personal information, the company will notify affected individuals and applicable regulators as required by law.' No timeline, no named role, and no description of what a notification must contain appears anywhere in the plan or its appendices.
reasoning: A commitment to comply is not a procedure, and this attribute requires timelines, responsible parties, and notification content, none of which a sentence restating the legal obligation supplies. A plan that would leave the responder looking up all three during the incident has not defined the procedure.

evidence_summary: The company has never experienced a data breach in its operating history, and has no breach notification records to sample.
reasoning: The pass criteria explicitly defaults to pass when no breaches occurred during the period, there's nothing to sample because the triggering event never happened. Apply the criteria's own default rather than treating absence of breach records as a gap.

evidence_summary: A Notion database lists every category of personal information collected, which system stores it, and which third parties process it, functioning as the company's data map, but it isn't formatted as a formal 'Records of Processing Activities' document.
reasoning: No over-literalism, the attribute asks for personal information types, handling processes, and third parties involved to be documented, and a maintained Notion data map does exactly that. The specific artifact name (ROPA) is typical evidence, not a required label.

evidence_summary: The company's single combined data-subject-rights procedure covers access, correction, and 'tell me what you have on me' accounting requests in one document rather than as a separate accounting-request procedure.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline cuts both ways, the attribute needs the described accounting-request process to exist, not to exist as its own standalone document. A combined procedure that genuinely covers accounting requests satisfies this attribute even though it's bundled with the access/correction process.

evidence_summary: The privacy notice instructs users to email a privacy address at the company domain to request an accounting of the personal information held about them. The mail administrator's screenshot shows that address is a distribution list with no members, and the client confirmed nothing forwards from it and no queue or ticket type exists for these requests.
reasoning: A documented channel satisfies this attribute only if requests arriving on it are actually captured, because the criterion asks how requests are captured and communicated, not merely how they are invited. An address that routes to nobody is a published intake with no process behind it.

evidence_summary: The company has never received a request for an accounting of personal information held and disclosed.
reasoning: The pass criteria defaults to pass when no accounting requests were received during the period. There is no sample to draw when the underlying event never occurred, so this isn't a gap.

evidence_summary: The signup form enforces required-field and email-format validation at collection, and the account settings page lets users edit their own profile data afterward; both are described briefly in the engineering wiki rather than a standalone 'Data Quality Policy.'
reasoning: No over-literalism, the pass criteria asks for validation at collection plus a self-service update mechanism, both of which are present and documented, just not under a dedicated policy title. Judge the substance of the controls, not the label of the document describing them.

evidence_summary: The data handling document describes validation at collection in detail: email verification, phone format checks, and duplicate detection on employer records. On updates it says only that 'candidates may contact us to correct their information.' There is no self-service edit path in the product and no written intake, owner, or timeframe for those contacts.
reasoning: This attribute sets a floor of two things, validation at collection and a mechanism for data subjects to update their information, so meeting one of them well does not carry the other. An invitation to get in touch, with nothing behind it describing how a correction is received and applied, is not a mechanism.

evidence_summary: An eight-month-old startup has a data-minimization review scheduled on its roadmap for next quarter but has not yet conducted one.
reasoning: Solo/early-stage proportionality applies here explicitly in the criteria, entities under twelve months old pass if the review is scheduled, since a periodic review can't yet have a first cycle to point to. Judge against the minimum acceptable design for a young company, not a mature review history.

evidence_summary: The privacy policy footer lists a single support@company.com inbox for all inquiries, including privacy questions and complaints, rather than a dedicated privacy@ address.
reasoning: Judge against the minimum acceptable design for a small company, the criteria accepts a published email, and a single monitored support inbox that genuinely handles privacy inquiries is a proportional substitute for a dedicated privacy mailbox. Structural absence of any contact channel would fail; a shared but functioning one passes.

evidence_summary: The complaint-handling steps (intake via support ticket, escalation to the founder, target resolution window) are described as a section within the general privacy policy rather than in a standalone complaint-handling procedure.
reasoning: No over-literalism, the attribute requires the process to be documented and cover receiving, investigating, and resolving complaints, not that it live in its own document. A clearly described process embedded in a broader policy satisfies the same substance.

evidence_summary: Submitted as the privacy complaint process: the customer support SLA, which defines a 24 hour first response, resolution targets by plan tier, and an escalation ladder to the support manager. Nothing in it mentions privacy, an investigation step, the privacy owner, or how a resolution is communicated to a data subject.
reasoning: A general support SLA is not a privacy complaint procedure, and a documented timeframe for answering tickets does not establish the investigation and resolution steps this attribute names. Privacy disputes route differently, are owned by a different person, and end in a communicated determination rather than a closed ticket.

evidence_summary: The company has never received a privacy complaint or dispute from a data subject, and so has no dispute resolution records on file.
reasoning: The pass criteria defaults to pass when no disputes were received during the period, there is nothing to sample because the triggering event never occurred. Don't treat the absence of dispute records as evidence of a missing process when the criteria already accounts for zero disputes.

evidence_summary: A GitHub API export (raw JSON, not a console screenshot) of the production branch protection rule shows required_pull_request_reviews enabled and allow_force_pushes set to false.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a live API export showing the substance of branch protection passes just as a console screenshot would. The format of the capture does not matter if it plainly shows direct and force pushes are blocked.

evidence_summary: The engineering handbook states from memory that 'production branch is protected and can't be pushed to directly,' with no GitHub settings export or screenshot attached.
reasoning: A client-authored description of a configuration is not system proof of that configuration. Branch protection is a config attribute that needs an actual GitHub settings export or screenshot, not a handbook claim.

evidence_summary: A cropped GitHub branch protection screenshot shows the 'Include administrators' toggle in the on position, but the rest of the settings page is cut off from the capture.
reasoning: A live capture plainly showing the substance passes even if it is not a full-page screenshot. The visible toggle is the exact setting the attribute tests, so a partial crop that still shows it is sufficient.

evidence_summary: The founder verbally confirms in the review call that 'admin enforcement is always on for the production branch,' with no GitHub settings export submitted.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config evidence. The administrator-enforcement setting must be shown in an actual branch protection configuration export, not asserted in conversation.

evidence_summary: Branch protection configuration for the production branch requires only a single 'build' status check to pass before merge, and the corresponding CI workflow runs on every pull request.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: the pass criteria requires 'one or more' required status checks, not a specific number or a comprehensive test suite. A single enforced, functioning check satisfies the attribute as written.

evidence_summary: A CI workflow file defining a test suite exists in the repository, but the branch protection settings export shows required_status_checks is null, meaning nothing is actually enforced at merge time.
reasoning: The mere existence of a CI workflow is not the same as the workflow being required for merge. The system configuration must actually show the check listed as required, and here it does not.

evidence_summary: For a solo-developer company, sampled merged pull requests show a description of the change and passing required CI checks, but were self-approved by the same developer who authored them, since no second engineer exists.
reasoning: Never import a neighbor attribute's requirement: this attribute only requires a description, passing required checks, and traceability, not a second-person approval, which belongs to a separate peer-review control. Judged against its own text, the sampled merges pass.

evidence_summary: Each of the three sampled merged changes has a clear description and a green status check visible on the pull request. On one of them the merge commit is timestamped 14:02 and the required test run finished at 14:41, having been triggered on the main branch after the merge.
reasoning: The checks have to pass before the merge, because a check that runs afterwards tells the entity what it shipped rather than gating whether it ships. A green badge read at fieldwork time hides the ordering, so the timestamps are the evidence, not the badge.

evidence_summary: The deployment platform's dashboard automatically runs a post-deploy health check and shows a green 'Deployment Ready' status with response-time metrics for the most recent release, captured as a screenshot.
reasoning: A live capture plainly showing the substance passes even without a separately written 'verification log.' An automated platform health check tied to the deployment is exactly the kind of record the attribute asks for.

evidence_summary: The deployment pipeline definition includes a smoke test stage with real assertions against the ticketing checkout path. The run log for the most recent production deployment shows that stage as 'skipped', because it is configured to run only when a manual flag is set, and no monitoring review or other verification was recorded for that deployment.
reasoning: A verification practice has to have been performed for a recent deployment, so a configured stage that did not run is a defined intention rather than evidence. A conditional gate that defaults to skipped will be skipped exactly when it matters, which is why the attribute asks for the run and not the configuration.

evidence_summary: A two-founder company maintains a simple shared spreadsheet listing each founder's laptop, serial number, and owner, updated within the past week.
reasoning: For a founder-managed environment the attribute's own note allows the inventory to be a simple maintained list. A current, complete spreadsheet tying each device to its owner passes on that proportional basis rather than being gapped for lacking a formal asset-management tool.

evidence_summary: The device inventory lists nine laptops, each tied to a named owner and updated last month. The identity provider shows twelve accounts with production access; three of those people appear nowhere in the device inventory, and two of them are contractors known to work from their own machines.
reasoning: This attribute sets an explicit floor, that the device count is at least the number of people who access production, so a well maintained list that is short of that floor still fails. Devices missing from the inventory are usually personal or contractor machines, which are the ones no endpoint control reaches.

evidence_summary: Disk-encryption command output was captured for both founders' current laptops in the inventory, but a third, older laptop that was retired and removed from the device inventory before the test date has no capture.
reasoning: Encryption evidence is measured against the current inventory, not a device already removed from service. A retired laptop no longer in the production-accessing inventory is outside the population, so full coverage of the two active inventoried devices passes.

evidence_summary: A founder submits a short written statement asserting 'both our laptops have FileVault turned on' instead of an actual command output or screenshot from each device.
reasoning: A founder-authored assertion is explicitly not acceptable proof for this attribute; the required evidence is the device's own command output or a screenshot of it. A typed claim with no real system capture gaps.

evidence_summary: Screenshots of each inventoried device's system settings show screen lock enabled with the timeout set to 'immediately,' rather than a specific minute count listed in a field.
reasoning: An 'immediately' lock setting is strictly tighter than the 15-minute maximum the attribute allows, so the live capture plainly satisfies the requirement. No numeric minute value needs to appear separately when the setting is visibly within bound.

evidence_summary: A founder describes in a Slack message that screen lock is enabled on all company devices, but no screenshots or command output from the devices themselves were captured.
reasoning: A written or verbal assertion is never a substitute for the device's own setting output, which this attribute requires. Without an actual screenshot or command result per inventoried device, it gaps pending real evidence.

evidence_summary: Update-setting screenshots show 'Automatically keep my Mac up to date' turned on for each inventoried device, but one screenshot was captured a week before the as-of test date rather than on that exact date.
reasoning: A persistent toggle setting captured shortly before the test date, with no evidence of any subsequent change, still reflects the as-of-date configuration. A minor capture-date gap does not undermine evidence of a standing setting, so it passes.

evidence_summary: A founder provides a typed list stating 'all devices set to auto-update: yes' with no accompanying screenshots or command output from the devices.
reasoning: A typed assertion is explicitly not acceptable here; the attribute requires the device's own update-configuration output. A written list with no real capture gaps pending device-level evidence.

evidence_summary: A draft onboarding runbook includes a line 'Access review cadence: TBD, review anchored on exports' with the rest of the document still marked as a work-in-progress outline with no owner or adoption date.
reasoning: A draft with an unresolved placeholder is not an adopted practice. A 'TBD' cadence means the practice does not actually state a cadence as the attribute requires, regardless of language elsewhere in the draft that sounds compliant.

evidence_summary: A two-person company logs its self-reviews as dated entries in a shared Notion page roughly every three months, with no formal audit-tooling export, but the dates show consistent quarterly spacing over the year.
reasoning: Judge against proportional practice for a small team: a consistently dated informal log meeting the stated quarterly cadence is a legitimate pass path, not a requirement for dedicated compliance tooling. The pass rests on the dated records showing reviews at the required cadence, proportional to team size.

evidence_summary: The access management policy states the founder self-reviews access quarterly. One dated review record was provided, a spreadsheet of all accounts reviewed seven months ago, with no review recorded since.
reasoning: The cadence the entity set for itself is the benchmark this attribute measures against, not the twelve month outer bound. A single review seven months old means at least one quarterly cycle passed with no review at all, so the practice as stated is not being followed.

evidence_summary: The quarterly self-review is based on a spreadsheet the founder typed from memory listing current employees and their access, which happens to match the actual production user list.
reasoning: A founder-authored spreadsheet is not a system-generated export, even when its contents happen to be accurate. The attribute requires the review to be anchored on output pulled from the system itself, such as an API result or admin console export, not a hand-typed list.

evidence_summary: An unexpected admin grant found during the quarterly review was revoked directly in the identity provider the same day, evidenced by a timestamped screenshot of the access removal, with no separate remediation ticket filed.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a timestamped system screenshot showing the access was actually removed is a dated record of remediation and does not require a separate ticket to be credible. The substance, dated removal of the unexpected access, is what the attribute tests.

evidence_summary: The most recent access review spreadsheet has a 'flagged' column with three entries marked 'remove, no longer needs access', including a former contractor's account. The identity provider export taken the week of fieldwork still shows all three accounts active with the same permissions, and no removal ticket or change record was provided.
reasoning: Noticing unexpected access is the first half of this attribute and remediating it with a dated record is the other half, so a review that identifies accounts and changes nothing fails. A flag that outlives the review is evidence the review is a formality rather than a control.

evidence_summary: The platform members export shows every member mapped to a role, and a former contractor's account is already removed from the org, but the capture was taken from the billing page rather than a dedicated members page.
reasoning: Judge what the evidence shows, not the exact page it came from. If the capture clearly lists members and roles with no former personnel retained, the source page it was captured from is immaterial.

evidence_summary: The admin said on a call that old members were cleaned up last month, with no members-list export or screenshot provided.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The role-restriction claim needs an actual export or screenshot of the current members list.

evidence_summary: The git integration settings show production deploys only from the main branch with required review before merge, and preview deployments run per-branch with separate environment variables; the screenshot doesn't separately label a protected-environment toggle, though the branch and review gating is visible.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a capture plainly showing branch-restricted deploys gated by required review, with preview environments isolated, passes even if a specific named feature isn't separately itemized.

evidence_summary: The client wrote in a spreadsheet that only the main branch can deploy to production, with no screenshot or export of the actual deployment protection settings.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof of a configuration claim. The deployment gating needs an actual settings capture from the hosting platform.

evidence_summary: The platform's own CLI environment-variable listing for production shows secret values masked and distinct from the preview and development listings, with no overlapping variable names, captured via the platform's export command.
reasoning: No over-literalism: separate, masked per-environment listings with no overlapping secrets between production and preview or development IS the evidence of scoping; nothing further needs to be spelled out.

evidence_summary: The client typed a spreadsheet of environment variable names claiming they live in the platform's secret store, with no captured export or screenshot of the actual configuration.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet of variable names is explicitly not acceptable for this attribute; only a real per-environment configuration export or screenshot corroborates the secrets-scoping claim.

evidence_summary: A live browser network capture shows a valid certificate padlock and a 301 redirect from HTTP to HTTPS on the production domain, but the file isn't formatted as a formal certificate listing export.
reasoning: Judge the substance a live capture shows, not its format; a capture demonstrating a valid certificate and enforced HTTPS redirect passes regardless of whether it looks like a formal certificate listing.

evidence_summary: The client wrote in a security questionnaire response that SSL is enabled, with no certificate listing, scan output, or screenshot attached.
reasoning: Written self-attestation without a capture is not configuration evidence. The TLS claim needs an actual certificate listing or endpoint scan showing validity and enforcement.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the Supabase project's logs dashboard and Vercel's deployment log settings shows both providers actively capturing authentication and admin activity, but neither uses the exact term 'audit log' in its UI.
reasoning: No over-literalism: a managed provider's activity or event logging that substantively captures the required categories satisfies the attribute even when the provider's own UI does not use the words 'audit log.'

evidence_summary: A client-authored table lists each provider (hosting, database, auth) with a checkmark for 'logging enabled,' but no settings screenshot or export from any of the providers themselves was submitted.
reasoning: Because these are managed services, a client-authored list of what is logged is explicitly not acceptable; each provider's own settings screen or export must be captured to verify logging is actually turned on.

evidence_summary: The hosting provider's dashboard shows log retention set to 'unlimited,' a non-numeric default option, against an entity policy requiring one year of retention.
reasoning: No over-literalism: an unlimited or maximum-available retention setting necessarily exceeds any finite defined period and should be read as satisfying the requirement rather than failed for not stating a specific day count.

evidence_summary: The provider's dashboard shows a default 90-day log retention setting, and the entity's own logging policy defines a 180-day minimum, but the AI compared the provider's setting only against the generic 90-day floor and not against the entity's own longer policy.
reasoning: Compare the configured retention against the entity's own documented period, not an assumed generic floor; a setting that meets a general minimum but falls short of the entity's own stricter policy is a gap.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the database provider's role permissions shows that only the service role can query historical logs and no delete or purge API is exposed to organization members, but there is no separate 'retention lock' toggle.
reasoning: A compensating combination of restricted read access and no exposed deletion path is a legitimate pass path when verifiable, even without the single named immutability feature the typical evidence describes.

evidence_summary: An internal IT note states 'no one can delete our audit logs,' but no screenshot of the provider's actual role or permission configuration was submitted.
reasoning: Verbal or written assertions are never config evidence; the provider's own permission settings must be captured to confirm logs cannot be altered or deleted.

evidence_summary: No dated manual log review record exists, but a configuration screenshot shows the provider's audit logs are piped into a monitoring platform that pages on-call staff for anomalies.
reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage: a live alerting connection that surfaces anomalies satisfies the attribute just as well as a manual dated review record, since the goal is that logs are actually consumed rather than left write-only.

evidence_summary: The provider console shows audit logging enabled across all regions and delivering to a retention bucket. There is no defined review cadence and no dated review record. The monitoring tool's alert rules were exported and cover application error rates and endpoint latency only, with no rule reading the provider audit log.
reasoning: Collecting a log is not reviewing it, and this attribute is satisfied by a review cadence with a dated record or by alerting that actually reads the log. Retention with nothing watching means an anomaly is discoverable afterwards rather than surfaced, which is the difference the attribute is drawing.

evidence_summary: A managed Postgres provider's dashboard screenshot shows point-in-time recovery enabled with a 14-day retention window and a read replica listed in a different region, but the capture was submitted as a plain 'database settings' screenshot with no callout of the region field.
reasoning: A live capture plainly showing the substance passes even if each element is not separately itemized. The dashboard already shows PITR enabled, retention, and a separate-region replica, which is exactly what the attribute requires.

evidence_summary: The internal runbook states 'our database provider automatically handles backups and recovery for us,' with no actual provider dashboard screenshot or configuration export submitted.
reasoning: The attribute's own pass criteria explicitly requires the provider's own configuration output, not a client-authored description of the arrangement. A written assurance about the provider's behavior is not the same as showing the provider's actual settings.

evidence_summary: An engineer states in the review call that 'we tested restoring from a backup a few months ago and it worked fine,' but no dated restoration record, dashboard export, or ticket documenting the test was submitted.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never a substitute for a documented record. The attribute requires an actual restoration test record showing the date, the data store restored, and the outcome, not a recollection offered in conversation.

evidence_summary: The restoration steps for the managed database exist as inline comments in the infrastructure repository's README rather than as a separately titled 'runbook' document, but they clearly walk through how to restore from the provider's point-in-time recovery.
reasoning: No over-literalism: documented recovery steps satisfy the attribute regardless of where they physically live, as long as they clearly describe how to restore the in-scope data store from backup. A README section carries the same weight as a standalone runbook file.

evidence_summary: The recovery runbook covers the managed Postgres instance thoroughly: point in time restore steps, who performs them, and a one hour recovery point target. The object storage bucket holding every published audio file and the managed Redis instance holding session and queue state appear nowhere in the runbook, though both are listed as provider managed stores in the architecture document.
reasoning: The procedure has to reach each provider managed data store the entity depends on, so depth on the database does not cover the stores left out. Object storage is usually the one omitted and usually the one holding the content the service exists to deliver.

evidence_summary: The AI provider inventory is a live Notion database with columns for provider, data categories, and sending system; the evidence pulled was a screenshot of that database rather than an exported document.
reasoning: Live system screenshots are valid system evidence regardless of format. The database plainly names each provider, the data it receives, and the sending system, which is what the attribute requires.

evidence_summary: Engineering states verbally that OpenAI's standard business-tier terms apply to the account sending customer data, but no signed agreement or DPA was pulled from the account or contract records.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never adequate evidence of a governing agreement. The attribute requires the actual signed agreement or DPA on file for the provider, not an assertion that standard terms apply.

evidence_summary: The documented training-terms summary for Anthropic cites the default API policy that inputs and outputs are not used for training, linking to the current published terms, but there is no separately negotiated contract addendum.
reasoning: The pass criteria explicitly accept identification referencing the governing agreement or the published terms in effect, not only a negotiated addendum. A dated citation to the applicable default terms satisfies the attribute.

evidence_summary: The AI provider inventory's training column reads 'No, does not train on our data' for all three providers, each citing the provider's public marketing page. No agreement, order form, or terms reference is recorded, and one of the three is used on a free tier whose published terms differ from the enterprise terms quoted on that page.
reasoning: The terms that bind are the ones in the governing agreement for the tier actually in use, which is why this attribute asks the determination to reference it. A marketing page describes the vendor's usual posture and can be accurate in general while being wrong for the plan the entity is on, and retention terms are missing from the record entirely.

evidence_summary: The subprocessor list discloses the AI provider under its parent company's registered legal entity name rather than the consumer-facing product name used internally, but the data categories and processing purpose match exactly.
reasoning: No over-literalism: what matters is that the actual provider is identifiably disclosed with its processing purpose, not an exact brand-name match. The substance of disclosure is present even under the legal entity name.

evidence_summary: The entity's own Anthropic workspace settings screenshot confirms the account is on commercial API terms; the provider exposes no separate training toggle for this setting because it applies the no-training posture contractually under those terms.
reasoning: Judge what the evidence shows given how the provider actually implements the control, not a literal toggle the provider doesn't offer. A confirmation from the entity's own account tier tied to the governing commercial terms satisfies the attribute where no separate switch exists.

evidence_summary: OpenAI's public policy page stating 'we do not train on API data' was submitted as proof of this organization's setting, without pulling the actual Data Controls panel from the entity's own account.
reasoning: A provider's marketing or policy page is not this org's own configuration. The attribute requires the entity's own account settings or export, not a general public statement of provider policy.

evidence_summary: The entity has a signed zero-data-retention order form with OpenAI, provisioned directly by the provider with no visible toggle in the standard console to screenshot.
reasoning: The pass criteria explicitly accept a signed zero-data-retention arrangement as an alternative to a console screenshot. The signed agreement itself is the required proof when the provider implements the arrangement contractually rather than through a UI setting.

evidence_summary: An internal security policy states 'AI logs are retained no longer than 30 days,' and this policy statement was accepted as proof of the provider-side retention configuration with no provider console or export actually pulled.
reasoning: An internal policy claim is not proof of the provider's actual configuration. The attribute requires the retention setting shown from the entity's own provider account or a signed arrangement, not a self-declared internal policy.

evidence_summary: The Admin API enumeration confirms the organization has exactly one active project, and that project is covered by the org-level no-training setting.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: the requirement is that every active project be covered, not that there be multiple projects. A single-project organization with confirmed coverage satisfies the attribute in full.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of one API key's settings page was submitted as proof that the no-training configuration applies organization-wide, without pulling the enumeration of all projects or workspaces under the organization.
reasoning: A single key's settings screen does not demonstrate organization-wide coverage. The attribute requires an actual enumeration of all projects or workspaces confirming none are exempt from the setting.

evidence_summary: The rule naming which data categories may and may not be sent to hosted AI providers is a dated section within the broader Data Classification Policy rather than a stand-alone 'AI usage policy.'
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: what matters is that a dated, version-controlled rule exists naming allowed and excluded categories, not which policy document it lives inside. The substance satisfies the attribute regardless of document title.

evidence_summary: Every hosted-model call in the codebase routes through a single internal llm_client wrapper that strips flagged fields (secrets, full card numbers) before the provider SDK call; a grep confirms no direct SDK imports on any other path, but no branded commercial AI-gateway product is deployed.
reasoning: An enforced redaction layer in the entity's own middleware satisfies the technical-control requirement regardless of whether a branded AI-gateway product is used. The pass criteria accept source code or middleware showing payloads pass through a redaction filter with all provider calls routed through it, which the wrapper plus the clean grep demonstrate.

evidence_summary: The codebase contains a comment reading '// TODO: redact PII before AI call' next to the provider SDK call, cited as evidence of an enforced redaction step, but no redaction function is actually implemented or wired into that call path.
reasoning: A planned or commented intention is not an enforced technical control. The attribute requires a working filter or allowlist that payloads actually pass through, not a note describing what should happen.

evidence_summary: A two-person startup's AI usage policy states in one line that customer data must not be used to fine-tune models without written founder authorization; the provider's fine-tuning jobs list, pulled directly from the account, shows zero training runs have ever been created, and no formal authorization ticketing workflow exists.
reasoning: A proportional documented prohibition plus account evidence that no customer-data training run has ever occurred satisfies the design requirement; a formal authorization workflow tool is not required when the rule exists and no run contradicts it. Demanding a formal ticketing system for a run that never happened misapplies the criteria.

evidence_summary: The AI logging inventory is a short README file in the repository listing the application's own prompt-log table and the Langfuse observability tool, rather than a formal governance-tracked asset register.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the substance of the inventory naming every active store, not on the formality of the document. The README correctly names both stores holding prompt and completion data.

evidence_summary: The entity relies on Langfuse's own configured workspace retention setting (90 days), shown in a settings screenshot, rather than running its own purge job against that store.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: retention enforced natively by the storing system's own configuration satisfies the requirement; a customer-run purge job is only needed for self-hosted stores that lack native retention controls. The tool's own setting is sufficient proof here.

evidence_summary: An internal policy states AI logs are retained for 30 days, but neither the Langfuse workspace nor the self-stored log table shows any retention setting or scheduled purge job actually configured.
reasoning: A stated retention with no enforcing setting or job is explicitly a design gap, not a pass. The policy claim must be backed by an actual configured control in at least one of the storing systems.

evidence_summary: Access to the Langfuse project holding prompt and completion logs is restricted to the two founding engineers via standard project membership, with no formal enterprise RBAC roles or groups configured.
reasoning: Solo-founder proportionality: judge access restriction against the minimum acceptable design for a 1-2 person company. Project membership limited to the two engineers who need it is an adequate access restriction at that scale.

evidence_summary: A policy statement asserts that 'PII is redacted from AI logs before storage,' but no sampled log entry was pulled to confirm redaction is actually applied to stored prompts and completions.
reasoning: Redaction claimed but not visible in a sampled log entry does not pass, per the attribute's explicit note. The policy assertion must be corroborated by an actual redacted (or documented exposure) log sample, not taken on its word.

evidence_summary: Two-person company; the non-technical co-founder, who does not write production code, receives a recurring weekly email summary from the CTO covering security and compliance status, evidenced by an email thread over several months.
reasoning: Judge small companies against a proportional minimum design, not against a formal charter or distribution-list infrastructure. A recurring documented email thread to a non-engineering co-founder satisfies the independent-recipient requirement at this company's size.

evidence_summary: Company founded ten months ago; no leadership or investor updates have been issued yet because the first update cycle is not due for two more months.
reasoning: An entity younger than 12 months whose first update cycle is not yet due passes under the attribute's explicit na_condition. There is no update practice to fault yet, so this is not a gap.

evidence_summary: Submitted as the most recent leadership update including security: the readiness kickoff deck prepared for and presented to the examination team. The quarterly investor update issued three weeks earlier was also provided and covers revenue, hiring, and product milestones, with no security or compliance content.
reasoning: This attribute tests the entity's own reporting line to people outside day-to-day engineering, so material prepared for the examination cannot be the evidence that the reporting happens. The genuine update in the same window is the one that counts, and it carries no security or compliance topic.

evidence_summary: Investor update's security section reads only 'Security: all good, nothing to report this quarter,' with no mention of risks, incidents, remediation, or compliance milestones.
reasoning: A line that names security without conveying any actual status is a generic mention, not substantive content, and the two must not be conflated. The attribute specifically requires status such as open risks, incidents, or milestones, which this content-free entry does not provide.

evidence_summary: A contractor sourced through a freelance marketplace was granted production access after only accepting the marketplace's standard platform terms of service; the company has no separate signed confidentiality/security agreement with the individual.
reasoning: A third party's generic platform terms are not this organization's confidentiality and security agreement, the obligations must run to the entity granting access. Crediting a marketplace ToS as the required signed agreement over-credits an artifact that doesn't actually bind the contractor to this company's security terms.

evidence_summary: A contractor's engagement ended and access was disabled the same day per the offboarding runbook, but the IT ticket documenting the revocation wasn't marked 'closed' in the tracker until the following day due to admin backlog.
reasoning: Judge the process by what actually happened to access, not by ticket-system bookkeeping lag. The revocation itself occurred within the stated timeframe; a same-day access removal with next-day ticket closure is administrative housekeeping, not a control failure.

evidence_summary: The quarterly access review spreadsheet has separate tabs for 'Employees' and 'Contractors/Vendors,' and the contractor tab was reviewed and signed off in the same cycle as the employee tab.
reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline means checking whether contractor accounts were evaluated, not whether they sit in the same tab as employees. A separately organized but equally reviewed contractor population satisfies the requirement that contractors be included in the reviewed population.

evidence_summary: A solo-founder company uses a free-tier uptime checker pinging its health endpoint every five minutes, rather than an enterprise synthetic-monitoring suite.
reasoning: Solo-founder proportionality: judge against the minimum acceptable design for a 1-2 person company. A lightweight external health check hitting production satisfies continuous uptime monitoring at that scale.

evidence_summary: An internal Datadog dashboard shows CPU, memory, and request-rate metrics for production, and this was credited as uptime monitoring even though no synthetic check or health endpoint probe exists.
reasoning: Internal metric dashboards without any uptime or health check do not satisfy this attribute on their own, per its explicit note. Resource metrics are not the same as an external check confirming the service is actually reachable.

evidence_summary: Availability alerts route to a shared team Slack channel watched by a rotating on-call engineer, rather than a named individual via a paging tool.
reasoning: The pass criteria accept chat or on-call routing as a valid notification target, not only individual paging. A monitored shared channel is a defined recipient satisfying the attribute.

evidence_summary: An availability alert monitor shows a 'triggered' event history for a past outage, but its notification channel field is blank, meaning the event was logged with no one actually notified.
reasoning: An alert that only records an event without notifying anyone does not satisfy this attribute, per its explicit note. Evidence of a triggered state is not evidence anyone was alerted.

evidence_summary: The only availability incident in the period was a 20-minute degradation resolved via a Slack thread with timestamped detection and resolution messages; there is no formal incident-ticketing system.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the substance of response and resolution being documented, not on the formality of the tracking tool. The Slack thread contains the required detection and resolution timestamps.

evidence_summary: The company communicates outage updates to customers through a dedicated Slack Connect channel rather than a public status.io-style page.
reasoning: No over-literalism: any customer-facing channel the entity actually uses to communicate availability satisfies this attribute, not specifically a branded status page. The Slack Connect channel is a live equivalent.

evidence_summary: The marketing homepage displays a static '99.9% uptime' badge, and this was accepted as the customer-facing availability communication channel.
reasoning: A marketing claim is not a live status communication channel. The attribute requires an actual channel that reflects current system status and can carry outage notices, not a static badge.

evidence_summary: There is no standalone post-incident-review policy, but the IR plan has a labeled line stating that any incident causing customer-facing downtime or data exposure gets a written review, with everything below that handled informally.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute requires the review criteria to exist in writing, not to live in a separately titled standalone document. The IR plan states a concrete impact-and-severity threshold that triggers a review, which is exactly what the attribute tests.

evidence_summary: The incident response plan devotes two pages to post-incident reviews: a template, required attendees, and a five-business-day target for holding the session. Nowhere does it state which incidents require one. The security lead said in the walkthrough that they run a review 'whenever something affects customers.'
reasoning: The trigger has to be written down, because a threshold left in someone's memory cannot be applied consistently or tested later. A well-specified review process with no stated threshold means nothing determines when a review is owed, and a verbal rule of thumb from one person is exactly what this attribute asks the entity to reduce to writing.

evidence_summary: The defined threshold is any incident causing customer-facing downtime. During the period the only event was a two-minute internal staging glitch that never reached customers, so nothing crossed the threshold, and no post-incident review was written.
reasoning: Apply the pass-by-default clause when it is written into the pass criteria: if no incident crossed the review threshold, the attribute passes on the defined process. The one event fell below the stated threshold, so the absence of a written review is expected rather than a gap.

evidence_summary: Corrective actions from the one post-incident review are logged as GitHub issues with an assignee and a status label, and the closed ones show a completion date, rather than sitting in a dedicated 'corrective action tracker' spreadsheet.
reasoning: A tracking attribute passes on any system that records the action with an owner and status, not only a purpose-built corrective-action log. GitHub issues with an assignee, status label, and completion dates satisfy the owner-and-status tracking the attribute requires.

evidence_summary: A section of the company's broader Data Classification and Acceptable Use policy states that production and customer data must never be copied into development or test environments; there is no standalone 'non-production data' document.
reasoning: A documented rule can live inside a broader policy rather than in a dedicated standalone document. A written clause clearly prohibiting production and customer data in non-production environments is exactly the rule this attribute requires, so demanding a separate document is over-literal.

evidence_summary: The seed script for the staging environment uses a fake-data library to generate all customer records; there is no separate artifact labeled 'masking configuration.'
reasoning: A seed script that generates synthetic records IS the seeding mechanism this attribute asks for, even though nothing is labeled 'masking config.' The substance, fully synthetic non-production data rather than a raw production copy, is what the criteria require, not the artifact's name.

evidence_summary: A staging database was restored from a production snapshot last month; an engineer says in the interview that they 'usually scrub PII after restoring' but no masking script or config was found in the repository or infrastructure.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. Without an actual masking script, job, or config to inspect, a raw production restore backed only by a spoken claim of scrubbing is a raw production copy with no verifiable masking, which fails this attribute.

evidence_summary: The company runs a single environment with no separate staging or development database; an architecture diagram and infrastructure inventory confirm only one environment exists, so the entity attests no production data has ever been copied anywhere.
reasoning: A corroborated no-copy attestation is a legitimate pass path for this attribute at the design stage. When an architecture diagram and inventory show no non-production environment exists at all, an attestation of no copying is fully consistent with the evidence and should pass, not be gapped for lacking masking proof that could never apply.

evidence_summary: The client attests that production data is never copied into development or test environments. The environment setup script submitted for the change control walkthrough restores the previous night's production database snapshot into the staging instance, with no masking step, and its scheduler entry runs daily.
reasoning: An attestation of no copying is only available where nothing in the record contradicts it, and here the entity's own automation performs the copy nightly. Raw production data landing in a non-production environment on a schedule is the exact condition this attribute fails, whatever the intent stated elsewhere.

evidence_summary: A live screenshot of GitHub's 'Installed GitHub Apps' page covers all repository integrations, and a separate live screenshot of Slack's connected-apps page was submitted elsewhere in the evidence set rather than combined into one file.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: live system captures are valid inventory evidence regardless of which file or folder they were submitted in. Check across the full evidence set for both systems before concluding the inventory is incomplete.

evidence_summary: The evidence cited is the identity provider vendor's public marketing page describing that it 'integrates securely with third-party apps,' with no actual list of this organization's connected integrations.
reasoning: A provider's marketing page is not this organization's configuration. The attribute requires this entity's own inventory of connected apps that reconciles with what its systems report, not a general description of the vendor's capability.

evidence_summary: A CI/CD integration holds a repo:admin scope in GitHub, which its setup documentation shows is required for it to manage branch protection rules as part of its stated function.
reasoning: No over-literalism: an administrative-sounding scope is not automatically excessive when the integration's documented purpose actually requires that level of access. Confirm the scope against the stated function before flagging it as over-privileged.

evidence_summary: A client-authored document states 'all third-party integrations have been reviewed and are appropriately scoped,' with no export from GitHub or Slack showing the actual granted scopes per integration.
reasoning: A client-authored assertion is not system proof for a configuration claim. The actual granted scopes per integration must be shown from the systems themselves, not summarized in a self-made statement.

evidence_summary: A solo founder logs integration reviews as dated entries in a personal task app, including a note that one unused analytics integration was disconnected after the most recent check.
reasoning: Judge against the minimum acceptable design for a very small company: an informal but dated, documented review that records an actual removal is a proportional pass, not a requirement for a formal review committee or ticketing process.

evidence_summary: Submitted as the integration review: a one page document the client wrote titled 'OAuth app review, completed', stating that all connected integrations were reviewed and found appropriate. It names no integrations, carries no date beyond the file's creation, and no export or screenshot of the connected applications page was provided.
reasoning: A recorded review has to show what was reviewed and what came of it, because a conclusion with no population behind it cannot be re-performed or tested. A self-written statement that everything was found appropriate is the assertion this attribute asks the entity to support, not support for it.

evidence_summary: A screenshot of the GitHub organization's security settings shows Dependabot alerts and security updates enabled as an org-wide default applying to all repositories, rather than a separate per-repository screenshot for each production repo.
reasoning: No over-literalism: an org-wide default configuration that necessarily covers every production repository satisfies coverage without requiring a repeated per-repo capture.

evidence_summary: An engineering wiki page states 'Dependabot is enabled on all our repos,' but no screenshot or export of the actual GitHub security settings was provided.
reasoning: A client-authored statement is not system proof for a configuration claim; it needs a capture of the platform's own settings or corroboration against a live view. The wiki claim alone does not verify the setting is actually enabled.

evidence_summary: An internal engineering handbook page (actively maintained, referenced in onboarding, not marked draft) sets remediation windows of 7 days for critical, 30 for high, and 90 for medium/low dependency advisories, but it is not labeled a formal 'security policy.'
reasoning: Judge the substance of an adopted, in-use document rather than its title; a handbook page that is actually followed and defines severity-differentiated windows satisfies the attribute even without a formal policy label.

evidence_summary: The engineering handbook's dependency section reads: 'Vulnerable dependencies are patched promptly, with critical issues prioritized ahead of routine upgrades.' No number of days appears anywhere, and no separate expectation is stated for any severity level.
reasoning: A window is a stated period, so promptly is a posture rather than the window this attribute requires. Prioritising critical work is also not the same as differentiating the window by severity, and with no number written down nothing can later be found late.

evidence_summary: Resolved Dependabot pull requests reference the CVE ID in the title and show the alert-opened date and merge date, but there is no separately labeled 'advisory record' document tying the two together.
reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing; the pull request itself, showing opened and fixed dates against a named CVE, is the underlying record the attribute asks for and should be judged on its content, not on the absence of a separately formatted advisory log.

evidence_summary: The SaaS inventory is maintained live inside a SaaS-management platform dashboard (showing owner assignments and a last-synced timestamp for each entry) rather than a manually dated spreadsheet.
reasoning: A live system's own maintenance timestamp is direct evidence the inventory is kept current, insisting on a manually entered 'update date' column when the platform's native last-synced field already proves recency is over-literalism.

evidence_summary: The inventory has a 'Data Type' column, but it is populated for only a handful of tools flagged as 'important,' while most rows, including several tools that plausibly touch customer data, are left blank or marked 'N/A.'
reasoning: Partial population of a data-sensitivity field for a few tools does not satisfy a requirement that the inventory identify sensitivity for its entries generally, especially which tools hold customer data. Crediting a mostly-blank column because a few rows are filled over-credits a weak artifact.

evidence_summary: A quarterly SaaS inventory review was completed six weeks ago (recorded as a dated changelog entry), and two tools adopted in the last two months already appear as rows; the evaluator fails it because there is no separate signed 'review sign-off' form.
reasoning: A process-exists attribute at the design stage passes on evidence the inventory is kept current, not on a specific sign-off artifact, a recent dated review plus recently-adopted tools already captured demonstrates the cadence is real and working. Demanding a formal sign-off form when the changelog and up-to-date rows already prove currency manufactures a gap.

evidence_summary: The SaaS inventory carries a review note dated two months ago and an owner for each of its 14 entries. The identity provider's connected applications list and the card statement submitted for vendor testing both show three tools in active use that the inventory does not contain: a design tool, a note taking app, and an AI transcription service.
reasoning: A review is judged by whether the inventory came out of it current, not by whether a review was recorded. The criteria fail an inventory that omits tools known to be in use, and tools adopted directly by a team are exactly the ones a review has to catch, since they are the ones no procurement step ever saw.

evidence_summary: Retention periods for customer data classes are defined in the same schedule already reviewed and passed under the data retention control; no separate DAT-05-specific document was submitted.
reasoning: The attribute's own note states that where a retention schedule is already maintained, the periods it sets for customer data classes satisfy this attribute. Demanding a duplicate standalone document double-counts the same requirement, so this passes on the existing schedule.

evidence_summary: An AWS console export shows an S3 lifecycle rule expiring objects after 90 days, matching the documented retention schedule, but the export itself carries no label tying it explicitly to 'the retention schedule.'
reasoning: A live system export showing an expiration window that numerically matches the documented schedule is sufficient proof of alignment. An explicit cross-reference annotation inside the export is not required when the configured window plainly matches the benchmark.

evidence_summary: A client-authored spreadsheet lists S3 buckets alongside a 'retention: 90 days' column, but no AWS console screenshot, CLI output, or API export of the actual lifecycle configuration was provided.
reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof. A configuration claim about live infrastructure needs an actual system capture or corroboration, not a spreadsheet the company typed itself, so this gaps pending a real export.

evidence_summary: One customer deletion occurred this period; an automated job log shows the deletion job completed on a given date, and a support ticket in a separate system shows the original request date, with the two together falling within the defined retention window.
reasoning: The requirement is that the evidence corpus as a whole shows removal within the window, not that one single record contain every fact. A job completion log plus a corroborating support ticket together plainly establish timely deletion, which satisfies the design-stage pass.
