evidence_summary: The public subprocessors page is live and lists every vendor matching the internal vendor inventory, but the page has no visible 'last updated' date, and the AI treated the absence of a date stamp as evidence the list is stale.
reasoning: No over-literalism: what matters is whether the published list substantively matches the vendors currently processing customer data, not whether a date stamp is displayed. Reconciliation against the internal inventory confirms it is current.

evidence_summary: The published subprocessor page lists seven vendors and carries a recent 'last updated' date. The vendor register and the AI provider inventory each show two further processors handling customer data, a transcription API and a new email delivery service added four months ago, neither of which appears on the page.
reasoning: A subprocessor list is measured against the vendors actually processing customer data, not against how recently the page was touched. The criteria fail a list that omits known processors, and the omissions here are the two most recent additions, which is the pattern a stale list always takes.

evidence_summary: Before a new subprocessor was enabled, the security lead approved it in a Slack thread referencing the vendor's security posture, rather than through a formal ticketing system review.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and use of the review step, not on the formality of the tooling used to record it. The Slack thread documents an actual pre-onboarding review by a responsible person.

evidence_summary: The team states that customers were emailed when a new subprocessor was added, but no copy of the notification email, changelog entry, or send log was pulled as evidence.
reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never adequate evidence of an actual notification event. The attribute requires a record of the notice itself, such as the sent email or changelog entry, not a claim that it was sent.

evidence_summary: The monitoring tool's alert rule routes outage notifications to a Slack DM the founder checks constantly on their phone rather than to email, and a test alert fired last week was received there.
reasoning: Judge the attribute's actual requirement, which is a channel the founder actively monitors, not a specific channel type like email. A Slack DM the founder checks constantly, with a received test alert confirming delivery, satisfies both required elements.

evidence_summary: A screenshot shows an alert rule pointing to a shared team support inbox that is checked sporadically, and no test notification or received alert was provided to confirm delivery.
reasoning: A configuration screenshot alone is not proof the founder actually receives the alert. The target is not a channel the founder actively monitors and delivery was never confirmed, so the attribute fails on both required elements.

evidence_summary: The founder uses a single status-monitoring integration that watches the hosting, database, authentication, and payment providers' status pages and pushes any change to their phone, but there are no separate per-provider subscription confirmation emails.
reasoning: Judge whether the founder is actually notified of provider outages, not whether each subscription took a specific enrollment form. A monitoring integration covering all four critical categories and delivering to the founder's phone is a subscription to outage notifications in substance, so it passes.

evidence_summary: Screenshots of the founder's email inbox show confirmation messages for hosting and database provider status subscriptions, but the evidence for the authentication and payment providers is only a screenshot of each provider's public status page, never visited from a logged-in subscribed account.
reasoning: A provider's public status or marketing page is not proof of this org's own subscription. Viewing a status page is not the same as being enrolled to receive its notifications, so two of the four required provider categories remain unsubstantiated.

evidence_summary: The incident log lives as a Notion database view titled 'Incidents' with one real entry recording date, impact, and resolution, plus a saved customer email draft ready to send.
reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute requires a lightweight log and a ready template in any reasonable form, not specifically a spreadsheet. A Notion database entry with the required fields, plus a drafted template, satisfies both elements.

evidence_summary: A lightweight incident log is maintained and genuinely used: three entries with dates, impact, and resolution, including one real booking outage. No customer communication template exists in any form; the founder said they would write something at the time if it were ever needed.
reasoning: This attribute names two artifacts and a strong showing on one does not carry the other, however lightweight the control is meant to be. The template exists to be ready before the incident, so an intention to draft one under pressure is the absence the attribute is testing for.

evidence_summary: No incidents occurred during the period. The team ran a dry-run of their process and wrote a short shared doc titled 'Incident Simulation Notes' naming a plausible root cause and one follow-up action.
reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and use of the practice, and the pass criteria explicitly allow a tabletop or dry-run note as the evaluation basis when no incidents occurred. The simulation note captures root cause and a follow-up action as required.

evidence_summary: The vendor register has an ePHI column and the data flow document names the same three counterparties (cloud provider, transcription API, EHR integration partner). No separate HIPAA-titled inventory exists.
reasoning: Judge substance over form: an ePHI flag on the existing vendor register plus a consistent data flow document is the identification this attribute asks for. A separately titled HIPAA inventory is not required.

evidence_summary: The data flow diagram shows ePHI flowing to an analytics vendor, but the vendor register's ePHI column marks only the cloud provider.
reasoning: A contradiction between the identification and the flow evidence fails the attribute. The inventory must agree with where ePHI actually goes, and an unflagged recipient is exactly the counterparty most likely to be missing a BAA.

evidence_summary: Three sampled customers each have an executed BAA. One was signed two weeks after the pilot began but states an effective date of the pilot start, and the executed pilot agreement already bound both parties to Security Rule compliance, subcontractor flow-down, and security incident reporting for that window.
reasoning: A documented interim arrangement qualifies when the required terms actually covered the entire handling window; here the pilot agreement carried the BAA content and the executed BAA is effective from day one. Failing this on signature order alone is over-literal.

evidence_summary: The client states every customer signs a BAA at onboarding and shows the onboarding checklist template containing a BAA step, but no executed agreement is produced for any sampled customer.
reasoning: A sample attribute needs the executed artifact for the sampled items. A process description or checklist template never substitutes for the signed document.

evidence_summary: One sampled BAA was signed three months after ePHI handling began. The client offers a dated email in which the customer agreed to keep pilot data confidential; the email contains no security obligations and no retroactive effect.
reasoning: A documented interim arrangement must carry the required agreement content for the exposure window. A generic confidentiality email with no security terms and no retroactive effect does not, so the late signature stands uncured.

evidence_summary: The AWS BAA was accepted through AWS Artifact and the client shows the Artifact acceptance page with the account id and acceptance date. No countersigned PDF exists.
reasoning: Console acceptance through the provider's agreement mechanism is the standard executed form of a cloud BAA. Requiring a wet-signature PDF is over-literal.

evidence_summary: An error-monitoring vendor receives stack traces that can include patient names. The client excluded it from BAA scope with a note reading 'logs only'.
reasoning: An exclusion rationale must establish that the subcontractor cannot access ePHI. 'Logs only' does not establish that when the logs carry patient data, so the exclusion fails and the vendor needs a BAA.

evidence_summary: An offsite backup vendor stores encrypted database snapshots containing ePHI. The client excluded it from BAA scope with the rationale that the client holds the encryption keys and the vendor only ever sees ciphertext.
reasoning: A vendor that stores or maintains ePHI is a business associate even when the data is encrypted and the vendor holds no key. The ciphertext rationale does not remove the BAA requirement; only transient transmission or receiving no ePHI at all can.

evidence_summary: The BAA template requires Security Rule compliance and breach reporting but says nothing about subcontractors. The client notes that in practice every subcontractor signs the same template.
reasoning: The flow-down obligation must appear in the operative terms. The client's practice of signing subcontractors does not put the required clause into the agreement, and the practice is invisible to the counterparty relying on it.

evidence_summary: The executed BAA incorporates the customer's standard BAA rider by reference. The rider, provided in evidence, contains all three required elements.
reasoning: Terms incorporated by reference are operative terms. Judge the assembled agreement the parties are bound by, not a single document in isolation.

evidence_summary: The access control policy has a break-glass section: it applies when the identity provider is down or all administrators are unreachable, either founder may invoke it, and the steps point to the vault entry holding the root credential.
reasoning: A section within the access control policy satisfies the documentation requirement. A standalone emergency access document is not required when the section covers circumstances, authorized people, and steps.

evidence_summary: The client walks through a sensible break-glass process in conversation and shows the vault entry it uses, but no written procedure exists anywhere in the policy suite or runbooks.
reasoning: The attribute tests documentation. A working practice described verbally fails it, because in a real emergency the people who know the process may be exactly the ones unreachable.

evidence_summary: A dedicated vault holds the cloud root credential, the vault access report lists only the two founders named in the procedure, and the root MFA device sits in a fire safe noted in the vault entry.
reasoning: The criterion accepts any secure storage form: vault, sealed credential, or hardware token. A restricted vault entry with a physically secured MFA device qualifies; a hardware token is not specifically required.

evidence_summary: The root password sits in the shared engineering vault that all eight engineers can read. The client notes it has never been used.
reasoning: Broadly available emergency credentials fail the restriction requirement. Storage in a vault does not by itself restrict access to the personnel the procedure names, and non-use does not cure over-availability.

evidence_summary: No emergency access occurred during the period. The audit trail shows zero root sign-ins and the break-glass vault entry's access history is empty; both pulls are recorded with their commands.
reasoning: With zero uses, the attribute passes on the logging configuration being in place, and the recorded empty pulls are the evidence of zero. Do not fail an empty population for lacking review records.

evidence_summary: One root sign-in appears in the audit trail during an identity provider outage. The incident retrospective describes the outage but never examines the emergency access session itself.
reasoning: Each use needs a documented after-the-fact review of the access itself: who signed in, what was done, whether it was appropriate. An incident retro that never looks at the emergency session is not that review.

evidence_summary: The data retention schedule covers customer data (24 months) and application logs (12 months). Security policies and the records of security activities appear nowhere in it.
reasoning: Customer data retention is a different object from security documentation retention. A thorough schedule that never mentions security policies or activity records fails this attribute regardless of how well it covers everything else.

evidence_summary: The policy governance section states that security policies and security activity records are retained for at least six years from creation or the date last in effect, whichever is later. There is no standalone retention schedule document.
reasoning: A sentence in the policy governance section is a documented requirement. A dedicated retention schedule document is not required when the requirement is written, scoped to security documentation, and reaches six years.

evidence_summary: Policies live in a shared drive with version history enabled, and the client opens a prior version of the security policy from 14 months ago on screen.
reasoning: Version history that actually produces an earlier version demonstrates retrievability. A separate formal archive system is not required when the repository preserves and serves prior versions.

evidence_summary: Policies are edited in place in a workspace tool whose plan limits page history to the last 7 days. The client intends to upgrade the plan.
reasoning: Retrievability must actually reach back to earlier periods. A 7 day history window cannot produce prior versions, and an intention to upgrade is not a configuration.
